items.title: United States of America
text: The US uses the phrase ‘**Speed Limit**’ on their speed signs.
The numbers on American speed signs are usually lower than on Canadian ones, since they use miles instead of kilometres. In addition, speed limits ending in 5 are more common in the US.
NOTE: [Canada](https://goo.gl/maps/zVYUCX62g3ENJct2A) uses the word ‘Maximum’ on their speed signs.

items.title: United States of America
text: Road signs in the US tend to use **more words** compared to their Canadian counterparts. A good example are railway crossing signs, which feature the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ on them. In Canada, these signs are typically blank.

This tendency is also noticeable on [yellow diamond warning signs](https://goo.gl/maps/ySfoRRrDjUqSRSub6). In Canada, the words will usually be on a rectangular sign below the yellow diamond, which would have a diagram on it instead.

items.title: United States of America
text: The US uses **American English** spelling (e.g. center, color).

In addition, the US primarily uses the [imperial system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units) for measurements. For example, speed and distance are measured in **miles**. You will also often see feet and inches on signs, indicating the height of bridges.

NOTE: This is useful to distinguish between the English-speaking parts of Canada, where British English spelling and (usually) the [metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system) are used. For example, Canada measures speed in kilometres.

items.title: United States of America
text: **Triangular yellow signs** with the phrase ‘No Passing Zone’ are exclusive to the US.

items.title: United States of America
text: These rectangular **junction signs** with a single or double arrow are found in the US.

NOTE: [Canada](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.7445702,-84.128801,3a,19.9y,168.72h,80.95t,1.15r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1se1gQJA3H13DWO2lWqmbwAg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) uses diamond-shaped junction signs.

items.title: United States of America
text: American **yield signs** are shaped like an upside-down triangle with a red border, a white field in the middle and the word ‘YIELD’.
NOTE: [Canadian](https://goo.gl/maps/zBwtzhBVjPgtw1628) yield signs look similar, but lack the ‘YIELD’ text.

items.title: United States of America
text: American one-way signs are usually a **horizontal black rectangle** with a **white arrow** inside of it. These signs will also always have the words ‘ONE WAY’ printed on them. In cities, they are a white vertical rectangle with the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them and an arrow underneath.
NOTE: [Canadian](https://goo.gl/maps/f9n6jHbEQJFrNY5e6) one-way signs are of the same shape and colour, but might not have the words ‘ONE WAY’ on them.

items.title: United States of America
text: Large highways in the US use large, rectangular, **green metal signs** with curved edges and white text to mark highway exits, distances to nearby towns, and the names of upcoming roads (mainly in cities).
NOTE: [Canadian](https://goo.gl/maps/JBuxw1mVSSq1cRy37) highway signs have a similar appearance, but will typically have squared instead of curved edges.

items.title: United States of America
text: Leading up to exits on large highways, you commonly see large, **blue rectangular signs** with white text, highlighting services, such as food, lodging and petrol, that are available at the upcoming highway exit.
NOTE: Canada uses [similar signs](https://goo.gl/maps/14FARb11GKUu4sBG6) on some of their highways.

items.title: United States of America
text: **Parking indicator signs** in the US are typically white metal signs with red, green, or black text. They may include specific information about when you can park on said road, and arrows indicating where parking is (or is not) allowed.
NOTE: [Canadian](https://goo.gl/maps/WWt6d3SRhG4B61Q19) parking signs use similar styles and colours, but typically are less ‘wordy,’ instead using more symbols when applicable.

items.title: United States of America
text: In the US and Canada, especially at large intersections, **long metal bars** with **stop lights** attached to them hang over the street. These bars also commonly have street signs, highway signs, or other signs attached to them.

items.title: United States of America
text: Thin metal signposts are common. They will typically either have several small holes or have a [U-profile](/images/united-states/u-profile.jpg?).

items.title: United States of America
text: Most states have unique, distinct and learnable [Adopt-a-Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adopt-a-Highway) signs, which can be seen on the side of roads. A map of those can be seen here. Keep in mind, some states have slight variations in design.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: United States of America
text: **Blue and yellow** shields are used for county roads, and can be seen in certain states in the US. Keep in mind, unique designs can be found in some counties in certain states. For more information, see [here](https://geohints.com/countries/us/signs/countyRoads).

items.title: United States of America
text: Guardrails, signs, and signposts are commonly painted a **medium brown colour** in US National Parks, which are often located in the west. Guardrails that are painted brown can be made out of both [wood](https://goo.gl/maps/syWa2BkK99zBRmzv5) and metal. [Rock walls](https://goo.gl/maps/bU1rFbRpVUP1LzRD7) can also sometimes be seen in place of guardrails.
[Here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_the_United_States#/map/0) you can find a map showing where all US National Parks are located.
NOTE: There are occasional exceptions to this rule, so consider other clues before guessing in a National Park.

items.title: United States of America
text: Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts use **small green and red rectangular signs** to mark the ends of bridges and guardrails.
NOTE: Not all bridges and guardrails in these states will have these markers.

items.title: United States of America
text: In Minnesota, these yellow signs with **vertical, black triangles** are placed before bridges at most major river crossings and at the beginnings and ends of guardrail sections on large highways.

items.title: United States of America
text: Wisconsin and Missouri are the only two states that use a **lettering system** (A - ZZZ) for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically have the word ‘county’ above the letter, while Missouri signs typically do not. The borders of the signs also vary slightly.

items.title: United States of America
text: Speed signs in Oregon often simply have the word ‘**Speed**’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.

items.title: United States of America
text: **Yellow** or **red** bands can commonly be seen around signposts in Texas.
NOTE: Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states, such as Hawaii.

items.title: United States of America
text: A horizontal blue, red, or green sign can commonly be seen at the ends of driveways in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula. The house number is present, in addition to either the **town name** and or the **road name** (usually).
NOTE: Nearby states often use [similar markers](https://goo.gl/maps/ETNAA9cvLDbB92Lw9), but typically lack any town or street name information and only feature numbers.

items.title: United States of America
text: Signs attached to **two** **signposts** can be seen in Michigan, Ohio, Minnesota, and New York. Not all signs are attached to two signposts.
NOTE: Double signposts can also be seen in other states, but are not as common.

items.title: United States of America
text: West Virginia sometimes features street signs with a symbol that resembles a **fraction** inside a **circle**.

items.title: United States of America
text: North Carolina commonly uses a style of street signs showing **street numbers** and **arrows** in addition to the street name.
NOTE: Other states occasionally feature street signs with similar designs, so use other clues before guessing.

items.title: United States of America
text: In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with **3 rows of numbers** attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections.

items.title: United States of America
text: These green **ATV Route signs** are unique to Wisconsin.

items.title: United States of America
text: Rectangular **white** signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.

items.title: United States of America
text: Rectangular **white** signs can sometimes be seen at intersections in Virginia.

items.title: United States of America
text: **White signs** attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.

items.title: United States of America
text: **Black** street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.

items.title: United States of America
text: New York and Vermont have **small rectangular green signs **with three rows of horizontal numbers. The top row of numbers correlates to the highway or road number the sign is on. For example, the sign in the image is on road NY-345.

Signs for Vermont will almost always start with 0 on the second row. The second row in New York will start with a number which corresponds to a district of the NYSDOT ([link)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/ce/NYSDOT_regions_map.svg) which will help with narrowing a region.

items.title: United States of America
text: In New Hampshire there will often be a **white metal sign** with the characters ‘**E-2**’ on it adjacent to the road, typically at either end of bridges.

items.title: United States of America
text: On some rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota, a **black-and-white marker** is attached to the posts horizontally. The shape may vary slightly.

items.title: United States of America
text: These **white reflectors** on signposts are unique to Kansas. They are most commonly seen on ‘stop’ signs in rural areas.

items.title: United States of America
text: Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that **hang from wires** that stretch across the middle of the intersection. These markers are commonly in yellow boxes.
NOTE: These are not completely unique to Michigan, but are most commonly seen there.

items.title: United States of America
text: Interstate 19 in Arizona from Tucson to the Mexico border uses **kilometres** on the exit and distance signs. This is the only part of the country that uses kilometres instead of miles for highway signs.
NOTE: Speed limit signs in this area still use MPH instead of KPH.

items.title: Botswana
text: Signs in Botswana are usually in **English**. Most town names, however, are derived from any of the indigenous languages spoken in the country.
NOTE: The Afrikaans language, which is closely related to Dutch and common in South Africa, is very rare in Botswana. You will almost never find Afrikaans place names.

items.title: Botswana
text: Botswana has a unique **black-and-yellow striped signpost**. More rarely, you can see red-and-white signposts.
NOTE: In Southern Africa, these signposts are only found in Botswana.

items.title: Botswana
text: These small **red-and-white chevrons** can sometimes be found next to the road.
NOTE: They are also very common in South Africa.

items.title: Botswana
text: Just like the other Southern African countries, direction signs have a **green background**.
The numbers of major roads start with **A**. These road numbers frequently appear on direction signs.
NOTE: Road numbers in South Africa never start with A.

items.title: Botswana
text: Some road signs have a **blue background**. This is an older style of sign that was used before signs with white backgrounds were introduced. They are relatively unique to Botswana.
Note that most road signs will have the newer white background.

items.title: Egypt
text: The official language in Egypt is **Arabic**. You can occasionally see it on signs in several of the trekkers. Its script can be identified by its lines and dots.

items.title: Ghana
text: **Black and white **striped signposts in Ghana are typically seen in cities. On rural roads, you will mostly see classic, non-painted, metal signposts.
NOTE: Black and white signposts can be seen in other countries as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

items.title: Kenya
text: Directional signs are **green **with a white border and text. They often display road numbers in white or [yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/DqEYtasj9mwbfE3G7).

items.title: Kenya
text: While infrequent, road signs in Kenya will mostly be **red and white**.

items.title: Kenya
text: Upon closer inspection of signs, billboards and posters, you will notice that the **county name** is often written. Therefore, knowledge of Kenyan counties can be extremely useful in region guessing.
_You can practise Kenyan counties using the quiz in the resource section._

items.title: Kenya
text: Post codes in Kenya can be identified by [signs in the format PO BOX XXX-YYYZZ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zkoZ8sYzmTGiRivA6), where the number YYY (usually 3 digits but sometimes 0) corresponds to a post code. This is the number which can be used to narrow down your guess. Often, the name of the city is listed after the PO BOX.
NOTE: You can sometimes see [PO BOX without the second number](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sNta3QHeJpwVVgoDA) after the hyphen which is not helpful.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it. Here is a _[quiz](https://www.super-duper.fr/quiz2024/areacodes.php?country=POST_KE&language=en&tile=gmaps&border=thin&difficulty=false&timer=false&gmaplng=en)_ to help practice Kenyan post codes_

items.title: Madagascar
text: Madagascar has two official languages: **French** and [**Malagasy**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malagasy_language), which is written with the Latin alphabet and contains many long, multiple-syllable words.
NOTE: [English](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1GZYGSBw3AdKn7CF6) can still be found on some commercial signs.

items.title: Namibia
text: Namibia uses **green** directional signs with the road number in yellow.
NOTE: Green directional signs with yellow road numbers are also used in South Africa and the other Southern African countries.
- Namibia uses A, B, C, D, M, and sometimes F-roads.
- South Africa uses N and R-roads.

items.title: Namibia
text: After the road climbs onto the plateau east of Kuibis, the landscape will seem mostly flat until you reach the [intersection with the D432](https://maps.app.goo.gl/LnyJcQw9FVFwQbiRA), but you can notice the road having a [gradual incline](https://maps.app.goo.gl/uKxxvnhYT7HLAqBk7) for long stretches. The soil around is very red in colour, with limited shrubbery or signs of life. The weather is clear, with some clouds far in the distance.

items.title: Namibia
text: Windhoek is by far the largest city in Namibia, as well as the richest, with many [high rise buildings](https://maps.app.goo.gl/2FUr1J4JEF7QN7D96) near downtown. Affluent and often gated single family houses are a common sight on the sides of hilly streets, which are often well marked with simple white street signs.
In the northwest of the city you’ll find the [slums ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SfddeDfHCm1tL2Ds6)dotting the hills.

items.title: Namibia
text: Gobabis is a big** north-south gridded** city in the desert, with** red soil** permeating the landscape and roads, which are very often unpaved. A faint green ridge is sometimes visible to the north to northwest. The [street signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yc9JLDVMMF9166Go7), while rare, are also green, with silver framing on the top and bottom. [Blue bins](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nEKjHa3Md6L2VEtr8) are also a good clue for Gobabis.

items.title: Namibia
text: The coastal cities of Swakopmund and Walvis Bay are **flat **and often have** sandy streets**, with **palms** and Norfolk pines planted around. Street and road signs often have [square-shaped signposts](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wrtSH3P4gsmkEgXy6).
Road angles can be used to line up parts of the city, but a northeast bound angle is common in both.
These [white and blue plastic containers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tqK6dNW6hqXnVhBR9) are common in Swakopmund, as are [yellow lamp posts](https://maps.app.goo.gl/8DgByYnCTwNfJgTG7) in downtown areas.

items.title: Namibia
text: Oranjemund is a well-off gridded city with almost exactly east to west streets, with an abundance of** planted vegetation** all around the city. Multiple [Norfolk pines](https://maps.app.goo.gl/P3Su4Jd2vpxZqgDCA) can be seen almost everywhere. Streets are well organised with E-W avenues and N-S streets, which can be seen written on [small blue markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/3pZrSDpLRb4ZCa5E6) next to the gates or on [street signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zQgR2ugtF3LkBsoZ7), which have varying designs.

items.title: Reunion
text: Being a French Department, you will see **French infrastructure**, such as [signs](https://goo.gl/maps/g4Zs8JkqkiWbQYt28), [bollards](https://www.google.com/maps/@-21.2427103,55.3131219,3a,75y,99.88h,80.84t,358.51r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sfAEf2UYNe56no-OLI1RWoA!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) and [poles](https://www.google.com/maps/@-21.281482,55.4317286,3a,90y,19.99h,96.64t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sm6b5qi8oScL85YCcGo5E_g!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu).

items.title: São Tomé and Príncipe
text: On top of the language, the Portuguese influence can also be seen in infrastructure, such as ladder poles and pedestrian signs with the same design as in Portugal.

items.title: Senegal
text: Being a former French colony, Senegal uses French infrastructure such as **bollards**, **poles**, **signs** and **road** **lines**.

items.title: Senegal
text: Most town entry signs in Senegal are white and feature a **thick pink** outline. The town is also written in a bold, black font.

items.title: South Africa
text: South Africa uses **green** directional signs with the road number in yellow.
NOTE: Green directional signs with yellow road numbers are also used in Lesotho, Eswatini, Botswana and Namibia. Here, the format of road numbers is useful:
- !!N and R-roads are exclusive to South Africa.
- !!A and B-roads are exclusive to Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia. In addition to this, Namibia uses C, D, M and F roads.
- !!MR-roads are exclusive to Eswatini.

items.title: South Africa
text: South Africa utilizes **triangular warning signs** with a red border and a white background.
NOTE: The four other southern African countries use similar warning signs.
!!Australia and New Zealand use yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.

items.title: South Africa
text: South Africa uses **white-and-red **chevrons. You can find a similar chevron pattern below directional signs.
In addition, unique-looking [small, thin chevrons](https://goo.gl/maps/UtnQqFLqBe9EupxC6) with one arrow are common next to roads.
NOTE: The thin chevrons can also be found in the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.

items.title: South Africa
text: A map of major highways in South Africa. On road signs, the **letter ‘N’ **should appear in front of the highway number. On Google Maps, however, the letter ‘N’ will not be present. Instead, a **blue pentagon** with the number will be displayed.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: South Africa
text: **Square, red stickers **on the back of regular signs are often found in Eastern cape and close to Eastern cape in Northern Cape and Free State. You may see them in the North West province as well, but to a lesser extent.
NOTE: Red stickers on the back of chevrons can be seen in almost every province.

items.title: South Africa
text: **White stickers **on the back of chevrons are often seen in the Cape provinces.

items.title: South Africa
text: **Metropolitan Routes** are major roads around cities. They are designated with the letter M.
These distinct and unique M route signs are commonly found in [Port Elizabeth](https://goo.gl/maps/ZfbwsNaUjonKnoAY9) (Gqeberha) and [Durban](https://goo.gl/maps/C94hkSvFEopmUoJx9), respectively.

items.title: Tunisia
text: In Tunisia, both **French and Arabic** are common. The Arabic script can be identified by its lines and dots. You can often see [bilingual signs](https://goo.gl/maps/gS1SqVNEC2RM3KPq8).
NOTE: The UAE and (more rarely) Jordan use English and Arabic.

items.title: Tunisia
text: Most direction signs have a **white** background with towns listed in Arabic and Latin script. The font of the Latin script is usually quite distinctive.
NOTE: Many direction signs include the capital Tunis, but this does not necessarily mean you are anywhere near that city.

items.title: Tunisia
text: Tunisia has a fairly unique **stop sign** with Arabic and Latin script.
NOTE: Similar stop signs can be found in Jordan and the UAE. However, Israel and Palestine use a different unique stop sign with a [hand](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cEbKb3viPzJEHuKS8) instead of text.

items.title: Uganda
text: Kampala is a fairly **busy-looking** city, with many signs, narrow **unpaved **roads and typically fairly small, one-storey houses. Like many African countries, houses will often be surrounded by tall walls, commonly with barbed wire on top.

items.title: Uganda
text: The city of Entebbe, southwest of Kampala, can often be recognized by feeling slightly emptier than most of the capital, with more **greenery **and somewhat fancier houses. The area also has significantly more **street signs** than the rest of the capital.

items.title: Antarctica
text: The tripod at the **south pole** can be recognized by numerous countries’ flags around the tripod, and a sign with ‘Geographic South Pole’ written on it.
This location is often on community-made world maps for a better scoring range.

items.title: Christmas Island
text: Christmas Island uses the standard **Australian bollard**. It is a simple white bollard with a red reflector on the front, and a grey reflector on the back.

NOTE: In general, road infrastructure metas are similar to those found on mainland Australia, such as [speed limit signs](https://goo.gl/maps/bMWYvWn1yBfSiWs29), [green sign backgrounds](https://goo.gl/maps/EDq64mntxxcKBnrk7), etc.

items.title: Christmas Island
text: Christmas Island is famous for its **red crabs**. Near Ethel Beach, you can find a trekker walking among hundreds of these crabs. Another smaller trekker where you can see crabs is [near The Dales](https://goo.gl/maps/deYXgd8DDC3RfBbd6), on the West Coast. Throughout the island, you can find [references](https://goo.gl/maps/jhXdg6Yp6Yo9LpMA9) on signs to these crabs.

items.title: Guam
text: Guam uses **green** street signs, unlike the Northern Mariana Islands, which use blue street signs.

items.title: Guam
text: Some Signposts near the town of Apra View are coloured **yellow**.

items.title: Northern Mariana Islands
text: The Northern Mariana Islands uses **blue** street signs, unlike Guam, which use green street signs.

items.title: Australia
text: **Give-way signs** in Australia have a white border and black text.
NOTE: New Zealand’s give-way signs use red, instead of black, text. Give-way signs are very rarely seen in South Africa.

items.title: Australia
text: Australia uses **white on black** and **black on yellow** chevrons.
NOTE: Chevrons in New Zealand use the same colours, but the yellow ones will have a thin [black border](https://maps.app.goo.gl/biUUqnrPGEgyF2HFA) and often, a speed limit.

items.title: Australia
text: **Green **signs with white arrows on either side can be seen at intersections which show nearby towns or cities. A number indicating the number of **kilometres **away the town can sometimes be seen.
NOTE: Whereas Australian highways have alphanumeric names (e.g. A2, C222), highways in New Zealand are represented as a number on a [red crest](https://goo.gl/maps/BvKMsNeuFMqAUriLA).

items.title: Australia
text: Australian speed limit signs have black text in a red circle on a large white **rectangle**.
NOTE: New Zealand speed limit signs normally do not have the white rectangular background.

items.title: Australia
text: **Yellow signposts** are specific to Western Australia.
NOTE: Although South Australia does not use yellow signposts for regular road signs, SA bus stops will have yellow posts.

items.title: Australia
text: Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are **flat **rather than round.
NOTE: These signposts are usually yellow in Western Australia.

items.title: Australia
text: Signposts in the Northern Territory can feature these **yellow **stickers.

items.title: Australia
text: Road signs with a **fluorescent border** are almost exclusively found in Queensland.

items.title: Australia
text: New South Wales is the only state to use **red ‘No Stopping’ signs**.
NOTE: All other states use white versions.

items.title: Australia
text: The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that** include text** are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.

items.title: Australia
text: **White **directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.

items.title: Australia
text: Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does **not **include an arrow.

items.title: Australia
text: This street sign is unique to **Brisbane **City Council.

items.title: Australia
text: This street sign is unique to **Gold Coast** City Council.

items.title: Australia
text: This street sign is unique to the City of **Sydney**.

items.title: New Zealand
text: **Give-way signs** in New Zealand have a white border and red text.
NOTE: Australia’s give-way signs use black text.

items.title: New Zealand
text: The majority of directional and warning signs in New Zealand are held up by **white posts**. Warning signs are [**diamond-shaped**](https://goo.gl/maps/Yc1aJRudbLkktBBQ8) and painted **yellow**.

items.title: New Zealand
text: New Zealand often uses **blue street signs **with white text, particularly in rural areas. While street signs of other colours can be often seen, blue is by far the most common.
NOTE: Australia almost never has blue street signs.

items.title: New Zealand
text: New Zealand uses **black-on-yellow** chevrons with a thin black border. [White on black](https://goo.gl/maps/mQzY6iFbA9iufm6N7) chevrons are very rarely used.
NOTE: Australia’s chevrons have the same colours, but do not have the border.

items.title: New Zealand
text: New Zealand uses **green directional signs. **If the sign is on a state highway, the highway number will always be shown in a **red crest**.
NOTE: Brown signs indicate the direction to landmarks, which can be useful when pinpointing.

items.title: New Zealand
text: Bridge markers can be found on most paved roads in New Zealand. If the sign is on a state highway, the highway number will always be shown in a **red crest** on a white marker. The yellow marker indicates the name of the river or bridge.
NOTE: Some bridge markers indicate very small streams or culverdens which can be hard to find.

items.title: New Zealand
text: The first digit of [Fonterra farm signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/iVEJfCaXqmsAC1qQ7) follows the regional pattern seen on the map.
_This image was provided by snowf\_lake and brainy. You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: New Zealand
text: The cities of Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch all have unique bus stop signs.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: New Zealand
text: There are many town and city specific **street signs **in northern New Zealand, which can be seen in this graphic.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: New Zealand
text: There are many town and city specific **street signs **in southern New Zealand, which can be seen in this graphic.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Argentina
text: Argentina typically uses **white-and-red** chevrons.
NOTE: Argentina is the only American country with these chevrons.

items.title: Argentina
text: T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these **yellow rectangular signs**, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, and the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.

items.title: Bolivia
text: Bolivia typically uses **bulky, white square signposts**.
NOTE: Peru typically uses black and white striped “zebra” signposts.

items.title: Bolivia
text: Bolivia has a **second official flag**, called the [Wiphala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiphala). It is a square patchwork of seven diagonally arranged colours. It is sometimes seen on government buildings and project signs.

items.title: Chile
text: **Slots** can often be seen at the top of signposts.

items.title: Chile
text: Chile uses chevrons with a **yellow base **and **black arrows**.
NOTE: Argentina uses white with red arrows.

items.title: Chile
text: **Orange street signs** can be seen at almost every intersection in the city of Lanco, and occasionally in the nearby town of Malalhue.

items.title: Chile
text: Villa O’Higgins can be recognized by the large **mountains** located immediately to the east. To the west, [snow-capped mountains](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QGUzYaHWvb8PphP99) are seen in the distance. Street signs, fences and many other structures throughout the village are made of orange-stained wood.

items.title: Brazil
text: Most Brazilian road signs have the backs painted **black**.
NOTE: This is also common in Paraguay.

items.title: Brazil
text: Brazil uses **yellow **on **black **chevrons, as opposed to most of South America, which use black on yellow chevrons.

items.title: Brazil
text: **Postcodes (CEP) **are seen frequently on [street signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wKc1PEDRwyae19DW8) in Brazil (though sometimes hard to read). The first two numbers will depict an area, a state or multiple states. The numbers go anti-clockwise from São Paulo, ending in Rio Grande do Sul.

items.title: Brazil
text: Street signs in [Campo Grande](https://goo.gl/maps/bP6rWChW4MMmzJS18) and [Joinville](https://goo.gl/maps/1UTu9TZ3KLZK4kxv7) are **stickers** wrapped around a pole at intersections. Campo Grande signs usually have extra information and a red and yellow stripe.

items.title: Curaçao
text: The coloured border or road signs can typically be seen continuing onto the back of the signs. These will generally be red or blue.

items.title: Curaçao
text: Blue street signs attached to the top of **yellow signposts** are common in Curaçao.

items.title: Colombia
text: Signposts in Colombia are made of white metal, and join to form a distinct **cross on the back** of signs.
NOTE: White metal signposts can also be found in Brazil, however these are usually wider.

items.title: Ecuador
text: Ecuador often uses a lot of chevrons in road curves (“**chevron spam**”), usually considerably more than most other Latin American countries.
NOTE: Colombia also occasionally uses a lot of chevrons in curves.

items.title: Ecuador
text: Ecuador uses a lot of **square road signs** with a white background, of the design shown in the image.

items.title: Ecuador
text: Sometimes, the back of the signs are painted a **teal blue** colour. The signposts are thin and made of metal.
NOTE: Ecuador is the only country in Latin America to use teal blue sign backs.

items.title: Ecuador
text: Ecuador uses these signs to indicate one or two-way streets.

NOTE: The [Dominican Republic](https://maps.app.goo.gl/NbmAmmV68vqXA6JW9) and [Puerto Rico](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7ihNZDn6wtVLZ1187) are the only two other Latin American countries to use similar signs with **text inside the arrow**.

items.title: Peru
text: Peru is the only South American country to use **black-and-white** striped signposts. In some areas, [black-and-yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/4X8W8dd1mmrbhVLH7) signposts can be seen.
NOTE: Uruguay sometimes uses black-and-white posts for its traffic lights, but not for road signs.

items.title: Peru
text: Peruvian metal signposts feature **concrete blocks** at the bottom.
NOTE: Within South America, Peru is the only country to do so.

items.title: Uruguay
text: Uruguay uses **thick wooden signposts**, which are typically painted white. They often have up to four rectangular notches at the back of the post.
NOTE: Thick wooden signposts can also be seen in Bolivia.

items.title: Uruguay
text: Like most of Latin America, chevrons are **yellow with black arrows**.
NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between Argentina, which uniquely uses chevrons that are white with red arrows.

items.title: Dominican Republic
text: Despite being located in Central America, stop signs in DR contain the South American “PARE”. Moreover, many signs are attached to **yellow signposts**.
NOTE: ‘PARE’ is also used in all of South America as well as Puerto Rico.

items.title: Dominican Republic
text: **Yellow traffic light poles** are typically found in the city of Santiago de los Caballeros.
NOTE: This only applies to traffic light poles - yellow signposts are common in both cities.

items.title: Dominican Republic
text: Street name signs in Santo Domingo often contain the letters **“ADN”**, a reference to the Distrito Nacional, which the city is located in.

items.title: Costa Rica
text: Like in Mexico, Panama and Guatemala, Costa Rican stop signs display the word **“ALTO”**.
NOTE: Stop signs in [Panama](https://goo.gl/maps/LaAjCE36HSZziiCg8) use a thicker font. Furthermore, in the rest of Spanish Latin America they say “PARE”.

items.title: Costa Rica
text: Many road signs have a distinct **cross **on the back. This is most common on diamond-shaped warning signs, while others are mostly attached regularly.
NOTE: Signs in Colombia almost always have a cross at the back, but they use white signposts.

items.title: Costa Rica
text: The provinces are sometimes written on signs, so they are useful to know. We will also refer to them in the clues below.

items.title: Costa Rica
text: The entire municipality of San José consistently uses these **green **street signs with a **white rectangle** containing an emblem. Calle/Avenida streets are numerically ordered, increasing from downtown outwards.

items.title: Costa Rica
text: By the entrance of Jardín Botanico Lankester, located southeast of Cartago, you can find a poorly maintained dirt road, surrounded by mountains in the distance, as well as a [sign](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ieKVnVBKyytKZxRw5#extra%5Btags%5D=aigen&extra%5Btags%5D=jardin&extra%5Btags%5D=pinpointable&extra%5Btags%5D=urban&extra%5BloadMode%5D=latLng) with the name of the garden.
Within the garden itself you will find a plethora of different plants, with the [walkways](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZeyMUPjpFPoufVLk9) having many soft curves, and almost never being straight.

items.title: Guatemala
text: Like Mexico, Panama and Costa Rica, Guatemala uses the word “**ALTO**” on stop signs.

items.title: Hawaii
text: Hawaii is the only state to use its own language, though English is still predominantly used. Most **place names** are in Hawaiian, so you can spot it on street signs, and other road markers.
- Hawaiian is a vowel-oriented language that only uses eight consonants: H, K, L, M, N, P, W, and (ʻ), called an [ʻOkina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CA%BBOkina).
- Every Hawaiian word ends in one of 5 vowels: A, E, I, O, or U.
- Each vowel can also have a [macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macron_(diacritic)) over it: Ā, Ē, Ī, Ō, and Ū.
These vowels are often combined to make [Diphthongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphthong). I.e. UI, AI, AE, etc...

items.title: Hawaii
text: Hawaii uses highway shields that resemble a **guitar pick**, with the numbers on the bottom of the shield. Most highway signs also use [yellow signposts](https://www.google.com/maps/@20.0269917,-155.6992435,3a,23y,129.32h,81.85t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s6nWi-67_zbEbhaLQER2TOg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?coh=205409&entry=ttu).

items.title: Puerto Rico
text: **Spanish**, instead of English, can commonly be seen on signs around Puerto Rico.

items.title: Puerto Rico
text: Speed limit signs in Puerto Rico are identical in shape and size to speed limit signs seen in the mainland US. The major difference is that these signs will always be **in Spanish**, instead of English.

items.title: Puerto Rico
text: Stop signs in Puerto Rico say ‘**PARE**’ instead of stop.
NOTE: ‘PARE’ is also used in all of South America as well as the Dominican Republic.

items.title: Panama
text: Panama uses the Spanish word “**ALTO**” on stop signs.

NOTE: [Mexico](https://goo.gl/maps/f1zLdwAo5VhYDhtC7), [Costa Rica](https://maps.app.goo.gl/K6pZqyNn2Hw52GXJ7) and [Guatemala](https://www.google.com/maps/@14.6255005,-90.5568668,3a,15y,74.14h,81.77t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1smSi97ivNOrtG5_baoEx9YQ!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) also use “ALTO”, but the font is thinner.

items.title: Panama
text: Red octagonal signs with an oddly **realistic eye** are unique to Panama.

items.title: Canada
text: Canada uses the word **‘maximum’ **on speed signs. Because speed is measured in kilometres instead of miles, the numbers tend to be higher than the US which can be identifiable from afar.

NOTE: The US uses the words **‘speed limit’ **on such signs. In addition, speed limits ending with 5 are more common in the US, and the ‘speed limit’ text takes up two lines versus one for ‘maximum’ in Canada.

items.title: Canada
text: Canadian road signs tend to be **less wordy** compared to their US counterparts. Good examples of this are railroad crossing and yield signs. In the US, these usually have the literal words ‘railroad crossing’ and ‘yield’ written on them, whereas in Canada, these signs are typically** **blank.

items.title: Canada
text: Canada uses unique **diamond**-shaped T-Intersection signs.
NOTE: Canada is the only country in the world where you can find these signs. The US, for example, uses rectangular** **T-Intersection signs.

items.title: Canada
text: In the US and Canada, especially at large intersections, **long metal bars** with **stop lights** attached to them hang over the street. These bars also commonly have street signs, highway signs, or other signs attached to them.

items.title: Canada
text: **Thin metal signposts** are common. They will typically either have several small holes or have a [U profile](https://maps.app.goo.gl/oqFAZpsUpMhbDx5P8).

items.title: Canada
text: French is the majority language in **Québec** and parts of **New Brunswick**.

NOTE: At the federal level, French has official status alongside English, so you can sometimes find bilingual signs in other parts of Canada. In addition, French is also spoken in several communities in Nova Scotia, Ontario and Manitoba.

items.title: Canada
text: Some provinces have **unique speed signs**.
Ontario speed limit signs may have a **black section** on the bottom with the words ‘km/h’ or ‘begins’ written in white.
British Columbian signs also include the ‘km/h’ but **lack **the black section.
Québec can sometimes have **French **on their speed limit signs.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Canada
text: You will often find these **yellow fire hydrant markers** atop signposts in Québec.

In [Québec City](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tXPTbFvb8CWHFhFa7) these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in [Trois-Rivières](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UZwuZs8zfPbjdAFX7) are distinctly small.

NOTE: Sometimes the markers will have [different colours](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dMcGqrRcNb4nB15dA). Beware that [Edmundston](https://maps.app.goo.gl/pD4sKaaLpPGWnWnw9), in New Brunswick, uses these too.

items.title: Canada
text: Québec T-Intersection signs **do not **feature the chequerboard pattern.

items.title: Canada
text: Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a **rectangular yellow border** around the diamond shape.

items.title: Canada
text: Road signs in British Columbia can have **green** backsides.
NOTE: Green backsides are also somewhat common on Prince Edward Island.

items.title: Canada
text: Signs in British Columbia are sometimes hung down from these unique signposts.

items.title: Canada
text: You can sometimes find a **green and white** striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.

items.title: Canada
text: Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these **white triangles**. The number can vary.

items.title: Canada
text: Stop signs with the word **‘Arrêt’ **are unique to Québec.

items.title: Canada
text: Stop signs with both **‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’** are most commonly found in New Brunswick.
NOTE: Such stop signs can rarely be found in other provinces.

items.title: Canada
text: Like the stop signs, street signs in New Brunswick are also bilingual.
Though unlike the stop signs, bilingual street signs are found in other French minority areas of Canada.

items.title: Canada
text: Rural roads in Alberta are numbered sequentially. This makes it easy to figure out your exact location using just a road sign.
- **Township roads** (Twp Rd) run east to west. Their numbers increase the more north you go.
- **Range roads** (Rge Rd) run north to south. Their numbers increase the more west you go. These numbers reset a couple of times.

[This infographic](/images/canada/canada_albertatownshipgrid.png) shows which numbers are found where. You need to multiply the numbers on the grid by 10 to get the road numbers. For example, the junction in the image example is found just north of Red Deer.
NOTE: Similarly named roads can also sometimes be seen in Saskatchewan, however they are more common in Alberta.

items.title: Canada
text: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this **pyramid** shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on [standalone posts](https://goo.gl/maps/hBq3pYWKuD2MkgFQ7) and [signposts](https://goo.gl/maps/grcv9vSj4wF5MUzZ7) as well.

items.title: Canada
text: Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a **diamond-shaped marker** next to them.

items.title: Canada
text: You can spot these **wooden boxes** holding up signs in Newfoundland and Labrador.

items.title: Canada
text: **Québec **is the only Canadian province that uses **red and white** chevrons.
NOTE: The rest of Canada uses the classic [yellow and black](https://goo.gl/maps/FQY3a1oqcfZTyGPs7) chevrons.

items.title: Canada
text: Iqaluit is the capital of Nunavut, meaning it is **more urban**, and built up compared to other Nunavut settlements. The city features bilingual **turquoise street signs**. Speed limit signs are also uniquely bilingual. And on the outskirts of the city, these unique road markers can be seen.

items.title: Canada
text: The remote town of Churchill in northern Manitoba features a trekker with a distinct thin **antenna **visible on the front right side of the car. The town also has unique street signs.
NOTE: This coverage is also seen in the surrounding area.

items.title: US Virgin Islands
text: Owing to its former status as a Danish colony, some streets and localities still have **Danish names** (e.g. _gade_) or display bilingual signs. This is most common in the historical downtown areas.

items.title: Bhutan
text: These signs are frequently found in the cities of Bhutan and are often coloured **red** or **blue**.
NOTE: As seen here, they will typically have the town name you are in written on them.

items.title: Bhutan
text: Signposts in Bhutan frequently have black-and-white **stripes**.
NOTE: Within Asia, these posts are also found in Sri Lanka, India, Nepal, Malaysia and Bangladesh. Make sure to check other clues before guessing.

items.title: Bangladesh
text: Signposts in Bangladesh often have **black-and-white stripes**.
NOTE: Within Asia, these posts are also found in Sri Lanka, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Malaysia. Make sure to check other clues before guessing.

items.title: Cambodia
text: Chevrons in Cambodia are **black with yellow arrows**.
Chevrons are somewhat rare. On many occasions, Cambodia prefers to use bollards instead of chevrons to mark curves in the road.
NOTE: Chevrons in all other Southeast Asian countries have the reverse colour scheme: yellow with black arrows.

items.title: Cambodia
text: Throughout the country, you can find distinct **blue signs** from the Cambodian People’s Party (CPP).
These signs occasionally feature the likenesses of major party politicians: usually [three men](https://goo.gl/maps/uWwgvxjSdKMp7W676) side by side.

items.title: Cambodia
text: Bilingual signs with **Chinese** writing can commonly be found in Preah Sihanouk.

items.title: Hong Kong
text: Hong Kong has two official languages: **English and Chinese** (legally, no variety is specified, but residents primarily speak Cantonese).
Bilingual signs are common, with English next to traditional Chinese characters.

items.title: Hong Kong
text: Road signs are white and rectangular, with a thick black outline and **bilingual **text.

items.title: Hong Kong
text: Give way signs feature a white upside down triangle with a **thick red** border and bilingual text.

items.title: Hong Kong
text: Hong Kong taxis come in two variants: sedans or station wagons, with the **sedans **most commonly seen. They can be easily identified by their silver roofs, green stickers on the front and rear bumper, and the taxi sign on the roof.

Red taxis are most common on Hong Kong Island and Kowloon, green taxis in the New Territories in the northern region and blue taxis on Lantau Island and Chek Lap Kok. Keep in mind, Hong Kong is a small city and taxis travel all around it.

items.title: Jordan
text: The official language used in Jordan is **Arabic** and can be identified by its lines and dots.
NOTE: Unlike the UAE, Jordan does not have English writing on most commercial signs. This can be helpful to distinguish the two countries.

items.title: Jordan
text: Jordanian chevrons are **white with red arrows**.
NOTE: You can use chevrons to distinguish between Jordan and Israel: the Israeli chevrons are black with white arrows.

items.title: Laos
text: **Stop signs** feature the Lao script. Sometimes, the sign features the word ‘stop’ in Latin script below the Lao script.
NOTE: In Laos, stop signs only have **2 characters,** compared to 3 in Thailand.

items.title: Laos
text: Within Laos, **blue sign backs** are only found in Luang Prabang.

items.title: Laos
text: Vang Vieng is also very **touristic**: you will see a lot of signs for hotels, guesthouses, and other tourism-related enterprises. In the (very few) rounds that the distinct mountains are blocked by buildings, this is a good way to recognize the town.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: Chevrons are **white** on **black**.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: Rather than having a word meaning ‘stop’ written on them, stop signs have a **hand** painted on them.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: You can often find this **yellow warning sign** on poles.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: These **white** rectangular signs with a thin **blue border** are typically found in Jerusalem.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: These **yellow** fences and signposts are unique to Kiryat Motzkin.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: Blue house numbers with the number written with [Arabic numerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_numerals) in the top left and with [Eastern Arabic numerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabic_numerals) in the bottom right, with a thin **diagonal line** between them, can be found in Bethlehem. [Street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/eouNa6SnvDgD8WQr9) will generally have the same format.

items.title: Israel & the West Bank
text: Roundabout signs which are either very **thick** or attached to a **large cube**, can be found in the city of Raanana.

items.title: Kazakhstan
text: A lot of Kazakh infrastructure, from pedestrian signs, poles, houses, to bollards, is very similar to what you see in Russia.

items.title: Kazakhstan
text: Street Signs in Kazakhstan are often attached to buildings and are **blue **in colour, with white intricate patterns on the top and bottom. They are usually **bilingual or trilingual** and can also contain a **QR code**.
NOTE: They are often inconsistent, with many designs being found in a single city.

items.title: Kazakhstan
text: Unlike neighbouring countries, Kazakhstan primarily uses **yellow and black** chevrons, except on T Intersections, where you will find the more generic [red and white chevrons](https://goo.gl/maps/PBScqLGeZf5WhaJa7).

items.title: Kazakhstan
text: While rarely possible, being able to read the letters under a QR code on a street sign will give you the region.

items.title: Kazakhstan
text: These street signs attached to buildings are generally quite inconsistent, but there are some worth knowing.
- Aktobe has compact signs where half of the space is taken by the QR code.
- Petropavl uses white signs, with a blue semicircle below the street names.
- Astana consistently uses this fairly generic design.
- Zhetisay also uses a fairly generic design, but it is not found in Turkistan or Shymkent.

items.title: Japan
text: Japanese is written with a mixture of **three main systems**: kanji and two syllabic scripts: hiragana and katakana. Formal signs and texts will mostly use kanji and hiragana. The kanji system is directly borrowed from Chinese and thus looks very similar, while the syllabic scripts are more loosely inspired by Chinese. Hiragana generally looks simpler than Chinese characters, many of the symbols have loops, which are not present in Chinese. The shapes are also typically slightly softer than the shapes present in most kanji.
_You can learn more about hiragana, katakana and kanji in the region guessing section, learning frequent terms and names._

items.title: Japan
text: Prefecture roads are identified by their **hexagonal-shaped** shields. The prefecture is often written under the road number in kanji. While the shield design remains, other variations can be found:
- On [prefectural highway shields](https://goo.gl/maps/6PsFbdz9gtDyGWbs9) (with kanji).
- On directional [intersection](https://goo.gl/maps/jsWfsJUW3r7JjE8v5) signs.
- Or on small, directional [arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/WrtbZh2DYQ6B4YYh7) signs.
As multiple prefectures can have the same road number, it is recommended to first find the prefecture you are in.

items.title: Japan
text: Some frequently seen infrastructure in Japan consists of:
- This unique [stop sign](https://goo.gl/maps/RYbbcM52HxH5rjvB6).
- A school [pedestrian crossing](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kp1Biy8pumCZtfsu5).
- And these traffic [mirrors](https://goo.gl/maps/RvMvRRrnmGWL4Z9CA).
While many infrastructural clues exist, these three are very common, and may very well help you identify Japan on a difficult round.

items.title: Japan
text: Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers you can find on their signposts.

items.title: Japan
text: You can find these **chevron-like** stickers, or more rarely orange ones, on guardrails** **in Hokkaido.
- On the [end](https://goo.gl/maps/9JKVotxnj4pqYvLz7) or side of a guardrail.
- Stuck to [metal posts](https://goo.gl/maps/iJBcacVCiaUCobVb8) between wire fences, which are often found in Hokkaido.
- On railings, which are often found on bridges, [underneath](https://goo.gl/maps/S75JPZKg6eYzrfAG6) the inside of the railing.

items.title: Japan
text: These specific **black **signs with **two yellow circles** are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them [stacked](https://goo.gl/maps/vu57GaqMEYEVbA8h6) on top of each other, or with an [arrow attached](https://goo.gl/maps/ijaCjxnsvDk9ohwZ7) above.

items.title: Japan
text: **Cyrillic **can be found on signs in the cities of Wakkanai and Nemuro, in northern Hokkaido.

items.title: Kyrgyzstan
text: This section of road goes through mountains that have **rocky cliffs**. These mountains are a habitat for lots of [spruce trees](https://goo.gl/maps/6ykqFWDntTbrPQnX6) that grow on the cliff sides. A more diverse selection of trees grows next to the river that follows the road. You can see that [some mountains](https://goo.gl/maps/ZYdKwBNtUvT3WQH8A) still have snow on the peaks. Most [signposts](https://goo.gl/maps/bRKCMi9bDmj5YCQV6) along the road are coloured blue.
NOTE: The southern section of the road features more rocky cliffs that cannot sustain any trees.

items.title: Macau
text: These **white** street signs with a **blue border** around the Chinese and Portuguese text are unique to Macau.

items.title: Malaysia
text: **BERHENTI** stop signs and **BERI LALUAN** yield signs are both unique to Malaysia.

items.title: Malaysia
text: This is a typical Malaysian directional sign. **Hexagonal yellow **highway shields** **are unique to Malaysia.

items.title: Malaysia
text: Signposts in Malaysia almost always have **black-and-white** **stripes**.
NOTE: Within Asia, these posts are also found in Sri Lanka, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh. Make sure to check other clues before guessing.

items.title: Malaysia
text: Malaysian postal codes are useful to know, since they can be found on most street signs in the country.

items.title: Malaysia
text: **Yellow street name signs** with a black outline are specific to the state of Johor.
NOTE: This **arrow-shaped** street sign, regardless of its colour, is exclusive to Malaysia.
NOTE: Yellow signs are also found in southern [Negeri Sembilan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HG89SePzMd5WWheo6), however only the tip of the arrow will be black.

items.title: Malaysia
text: **Green** street signs that form an arrow shape and have a **yellow hexagonal symbol **with the letters** JKR** on the left side are found in Sabah.

items.title: Singapore
text: All street name signs in Singapore follow this **unique format**. They are green, with rounded edges and a distinct white font.

items.title: Singapore
text: Directional signs are also **green**, with white letters and English writing.
NOTE: Expressways each have a **three-letter code** (e.g. TPE), making them easy to spot on signs.

items.title: Singapore
text: Road signs in Singapore are unique in that they are always set on a **square white background**.
NOTE: Road signs in almost all other countries will not have this square background.

items.title: Singapore
text: Many streets are named after the neighbourhood they are in, especially in the suburbs.

NOTE: These neighbourhood names appear very quickly on the map, so you can save yourself a lot of time scanning for 5k’s that way. For example, the sign in the image refers to Street 31 in the neighbourhood of Ang Mo Kio.

items.title: Singapore
text: You can easily recognise the **island of Sentosa** thanks to the green signposts, winding roads and general resort feel. Occasionally you might see a green lane like [this](https://goo.gl/maps/hrc9MLAc4F6GQihy5) as well.

items.title: South Korea
text: Triangular warning signs have a **yellow** **background**.
Note that circular prohibition signs, such as speed signs, have a white background. Yield signs also have a white background.

items.title: South Korea
text: Street signs will be blue, **arrow-shaped** and commonly **hanging** from a metal bar mounted to utility poles.

items.title: South Korea
text: Direction signs in South Korea have white text on a green background.

items.title: South Korea
text: South Korean pedestrian crossing signs can be easily recognised from the distinct **pentagonal shape** combined with the blue background.

items.title: South Korea
text: House numbers in the Hampyeong region can be recognised from the **large white section** at the top of the sign.

items.title: Qatar
text: Qatar uses **white on red** and **white on blue** chevrons.

items.title: Qatar
text: Qatari crossing signs feature a man in a [**thobe**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thawb).

items.title: Qatar
text: Qatar is divided into municipalities, further divided into **numbered zones**, which can be seen on [street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/M8fdWeriuhXw3Meu5). This infographic shows which number corresponds to each zone.

items.title: Qatar
text: **Brown **street signs, often fixed to the ground, are seen in Education City.

items.title: Philippines
text: Chevrons are typically **red on white**.

items.title: Philippines
text: Sign posts are often painted **red**, **orange** or **yellow**.

items.title: Philippines
text: Although Filipino is the official language of the Philippines, **English** is extremely common to find on signs. It is the only major Southeast Asian country where you’re likely to come across English.

items.title: Philippines
text: **Province names** are very common to find on signs and can thus be very useful. However, they do not appear on the map, meaning they’re necessary to memorise in order to use them.
It is worth mentioning that Davao de Oro changed its name from Compostela Valley in 2019.

items.title: Sri Lanka
text: Sri Lanka commonly uses **black and white** striped signposts.
NOTE: Within South and Southeast Asia, such signposts are also found in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Malaysia.

items.title: Sri Lanka
text: The country is majority **Buddhist**: 70% of the population practise this religion. Throughout the country, you will often see signs of the religion, including temples, Buddha statues, [stupas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stupa) and the [Buddhist flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_flag).
NOTE: Thailand, Cambodia and Laos are also majority Buddhist.

items.title: Sri Lanka
text: The presence of the **Tamil script** is strongly correlated with the distribution of Hinduism (though not all Tamils are Hindu and vice versa).
There are two groups that use the Tamil script:
- Native Sri Lankan Tamils, who predominantly live in the north and the east.
- Indian Tamils, who mostly live in and around the central Nuwara Eliya district.

Note that it is not uncommon to find bilingual Sinhala and Tamil signs far outside the area where Tamil is the predominant language. However, Tamil-only signage can be a strong indicator for one of the Tamil-majority areas.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Mongolia
text: Mongolian infrastructure has clear Russian influence. Wooden poles with supporting stone blocks, [white lamp posts](https://www.google.com/maps/@46.677839,113.270184,3a,64.1y,330.3h,92.79t/data=!3m4!1e1!3m2!1sAv0lfNtDl5QLj3rxCnkYzA!2e0), and [three-striped** **pedestrian crossing signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.2393538,106.2025013,2a,60y,95.51h,75.52t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sXUNd4wtT71dkoiStvdsI-Q!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) are common to see.

Unique to Mongolia is the** **[**“ЗОГС”**](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.2286946,106.2131419,2a,15y,73.91h,86.02t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sDbSJ2KjqHFeQw_Vx-Muhyg!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu)** stop sign**.
NOTE: Each town has unique lamp post designs, so learning them can be quite useful.

items.title: Mongolia
text: Choibalsan is the only major city to have several **concrete roads**. In most parts of the city there is a visible **smoke stack**, which is in the southeast corner of the city. It appears to have just rained as the roads are slightly wet and the sky is overcast. Additionally, you may occasionally find [unique pedestrian signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@48.071051,114.53028,3a,17.5y,333.1h,85.63t/data=!3m4!1e1!3m2!1srKpPHHlyC9nza3yV3IaZ3w!2e0) with a short figure over three stripes.

items.title: Mongolia
text: The desert town of Zamiin-Uud on the border with China has unique **sailboat lamp posts **featuring a** golden flower pot** around them. Often, white signs with Mongolian folded script can be seen attached to these lamp posts.

NOTE: The other desert towns of Choir and Sainshand look similar to Zamiin-Uud and have the same Street View car but use different lamp posts. Choir can be identified by its [blue](https://www.google.com/maps/@46.356902,108.371902,3a,110.3y,325.7h,98.24t/data=!3m4!1e1!3m2!1s6djXgVDAZ-fDj71h8NhXQA!2e0) lamp posts and Sainshand by its [white](https://www.google.com/maps/@44.893259,110.142104,3a,76.1y,92.3h,99.02t/data=!3m4!1e1!3m2!1sQ5CKt2u89UjuWb7RAyy5ig!2e0) lamp posts.

items.title: Oman
text: The official language in Oman is **Arabic**.
NOTE: Due to high tourism, signs in Oman often have English writing alongside Arabic. The same also applies to the UAE.

items.title: Oman
text: Directional signs are** blue with white text** and are usually in **Arabic and English**.
NOTE: The UAE and Qatar use similar signs.

items.title: Oman
text: Many signposts in Oman have **black-and-white stripes**.
NOTE: Within the Middle East, striped signposts are only found in Oman and the UAE.

items.title: Oman
text: Oman uses **black-and-yellow **chevrons that have an unusually large number of arrows.

items.title: Oman
text: Bins in Muscat governorate often have white-and-red chevron-like stickers on the sides.

items.title: Oman
text: The road southeast of Ubar has a general northwest bound angle, along with a power line to the left of the road. You will often see signs of life in the form of farms or buildings on this road.

NOTE: Don’t mix this up with the 37, which has a similar angle, but is [more desolate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/8uU7Jw947G7wktyd7) and can have [sunset coverage](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dD63F9RyzyfugxBw9).

items.title: United Arab Emirates
text: The official language in the UAE is Arabic. Its script can be identified by its **lines and dots**.
NOTE: Due to high tourism, signs in the UAE often have English writing alongside Arabic. While this is also common in Qatar and Oman, it is not common in Jordan.

items.title: United Arab Emirates
text: Many signposts in the UAE have **black-and-white stripes**.
NOTE: Within the Middle East, striped signposts are also found in Oman.

items.title: United Arab Emirates
text: These **blue** street name signs, with a narrow **metal border**, are specific to Dubai.

items.title: Nepal
text: Nepal uses black-and-white striped signposts.
NOTE: Within South and Southeast Asia, India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Malaysia also use black-and-white striped signposts.

items.title: Taiwan
text: Taiwan uses **black on yellow** chevrons.

items.title: Taiwan
text: These signs indicate Township roads, with the character written **before** or **above** the road number indicating the county.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Taiwan
text: These **bent** sign and chevron holders with two **black and yellow**-striped stickers are only found in Pingtung, Kaohsiung, and Taitung.

items.title: Turkey
text: Turkish chevrons are typically **red on white**. Beware that there are some other [regional variants](https://goo.gl/maps/c53U4ydsoRYVxGhk9).
Usually, the tip of the arrow does not touch the edge of the chevron. Some chevrons have a [neon yellow border](https://goo.gl/maps/h52NSmYxDJA77zVD8).

items.title: Turkey
text: On intersections, you can often find this distinctive **black and yellow** chevron, with multiple arrows that point upward.

items.title: Turkey
text: Sometimes, you can see these **narrow chevrons** that have a red and white colour scheme.

NOTE: Almost identical chevrons can be found in [South Africa](https://www.google.com/maps/@-31.9255787,26.9327084,3a,15y,260.14h,77.09t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1safeEbQeUOh2C-t3z0hfx6Q!2e0!5s20230401T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu).

items.title: Turkey
text: Direction signs use a very distinct font that can often be recognised by the noticeably **wide letter spaces**.

items.title: Turkey
text: Stop signs have the word “**DUR**” written on them. This is unique to Turkey.

items.title: Turkey
text: The third type of roads are provincial roads. While these generally aren’t labelled on the map, they can still be used to regionguess since the kilometre markers feature the [**provincial code**](https://sites.google.com/site/roadnumberingsystems/home/countries/turkey?authuser=0) as the first two digits on the sign. These codes generally increase alphabetically from 01 to 76 with some newer regions being unordered. Shown in the image is a road from the Afyon Province (03).

items.title: Turkey
text: **Yellow on black chevrons** are mainly found in and around the Balıkesir Province in the west and in the [Kars Province](https://www.google.com/maps/@40.7194663,43.1857553,3a,15y,58.93h,86.15t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1scyws6VGByT2Y02WeHnA4dw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) in the far east. Beware that you may very rarely find them [elsewhere](https://goo.gl/maps/bQYsRcd5eqHj3x1h7).

items.title: Turkey
text: **Black on yellow chevrons** are mainly found north of Izmir.

items.title: Turkey
text: Street signs in the Ankara Province are blue with a small **round top**. Similar street signs can very rarely be found in [Giresun](https://goo.gl/maps/aVtMnDJsqJ1ms4jf6).

Beware that some [newer street signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@39.9941773,32.8704415,3a,15y,27.52h,88.69t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sHNDiTJyKaZv36GFlgPI6wg!2e0!5s20221101T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) are red.

items.title: Turkey
text: Street signs in the Izmir Province are dark blue, noticeably **bulge outwards** and very commonly have the **emblem** of Izmir in white at the top of the sign.

items.title: Turkey
text: These light blue and grey **touristic signs** which are either arrow shaped or rectangular with a half circle on the top can be found on the island of Bozcaada.

items.title: Turkey
text: Red street signs with a coloured bottom strip are found in several cities. In the bottom right corner, you can find a white arrow and some numbers. If this arrow is pointing in **both directions** and has a **single arrowhead**, rather than [double](https://goo.gl/maps/Fd5tuzksA3NY8YsF7), then you are almost certainly in Istanbul.

Beware that simple arrows pointing in only one direction can be found in both [Istanbul](https://goo.gl/maps/6uFmLFqcEn2bT7vL9) and in [other cities](https://goo.gl/maps/BBU6aeQ2BoBN38YH8). However, if you see such signs in combination with [red house numbers](https://goo.gl/maps/kjNkwByQZ7rNaQXdA), then you should be in Istanbul.

items.title: Turkey
text: Street signs in Trabzon and [Yalvaç](https://goo.gl/maps/vZmpbacvJeyzbMWc9) are **red** and **oval-shaped**. [House numbers](https://goo.gl/maps/96X34Wg24K87jPG4A) also feature the same design.

items.title: Turkey
text: Street signs in Bursa are **green**, and generally have slightly **extruded letters**, meaning the signs are not completely flat.
NOTE: Several other types of infrastructure in Bursa, such as [fences](https://goo.gl/maps/EHzDyAUKLCQySbyB7) and [guardrails](https://goo.gl/maps/nF72j1rxibsT8weR8), may also be coloured green.

items.title: Turkey
text: Street signs in Bolu are also **green**, but are **completely flat** and lack any kind of border.

items.title: Thailand
text: Signposts in Thailand are square and bulky in shape, usually white, and often have the **bottom painted black**.
NOTE: In Southeast Asia, this design is unique to Thailand.

items.title: Thailand
text: Directional signs on smaller roads are **white**, and are composed of two signs: one with an arrow at the bottom, and one with the information at the top. These can have place names. When they do not, you will see them as just the road number with a [Garuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emblem_of_Thailand). Moreover, highway signs are **green**, and frequently feature the place names in Latin script below the Thai name.

items.title: Thailand
text: Stop signs in Thailand feature the **Thai script**, instead of Latin.
NOTE: Stop signs in Laos feature the Lao script, similar to Thai, but they have just 2 characters instead of 3.

items.title: Thailand
text: These distinctive **green **signs can be found all around Thailand, often in small villages.
NOTE: You will not find this sign in any other country.

items.title: Thailand
text: Waystones and road signs on provincial roads will often provide a **two-letter abbreviation** of the province in Thai script. They will not appear on waystones or road signs for national roads.
You can use [this](https://super-duper.fr/country/thailand_provinces_en.php) site to view and practice all province abbreviations.

items.title: Thailand
text: The majority of **Muslims** in Thailand live in the very south of the country. In these areas, you will often see Islamic religious attire, [Jawi script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawi_script), based on the Arabic script, on [signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/oy83kvBm8XWcc3ZEA) and mosques.

items.title: Thailand
text: Street signs with a **smaller** **green section** underneath a blue section are found in Bangkok and Nonthaburi.

items.title: Thailand
text: Street signs shaped like a **helm **are exclusive to Pattaya City.

items.title: Thailand
text: **Red street signs** with golden decorated borders can be found in Mueang Chiang Rai.
NOTE: It is possible to see blue street signs with the same border in the city.

items.title: Andorra
text: Pedestrian signs** **have **8 stripes**.
NOTE: Spain is the only other European country that has pedestrian signs with 8 stripes.

items.title: Belarus
text: Signs will be in Belarusian or Russian. Both languages use the Cyrillic alphabet.
NOTE: The letters ў and і are not found in Russian.

items.title: Belarus
text: The Minsk centre street signs are **sea-green**, and can be seen almost everywhere.
NOTE: If you are close enough to the sign, you can make out the Cyrillic letters “вул (vul)”, the Belarusian name for “street”.

items.title: Azores
text: Since the Azores is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles, chevrons and bollards.

items.title: Azores
text: Street signs in the Azores are almost exclusively painted ceramic tiles, with blue letters and, typically, a decorative pattern around the edge.

items.title: Azores
text: Signposts on the Azores are often striped.
NOTE: These are also seen on Madeira.

items.title: Albania
text: Albanian chevrons are **white on black**.
NOTE: Within southern Europe this chevron is also used by Italy, Greece, and Spain.
Montenegro uses two chevrons, both of which are different from the Albanian chevron: black on white and red on yellow.

items.title: Albania
text: The backs of road signs are often painted **black**.
NOTE: This is also common in Italy and Romania.

items.title: Albania
text: The “S” on Albanian stop signs feature a **distinct shape**; the ends of the S are quite short and have the same angle as the middle, rather than being vertical. This is also sometimes seen on [directional signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@41.4762807,19.7144537,3a,15y,293.79h,86.16t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s0Xem3meAWDPpNUbSfeuE5A!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu).
NOTE: Italian [stops signs](https://goo.gl/maps/366KjYZAnUyXk4YZ6) and [directional signs](https://goo.gl/maps/EKJL6bTozCYSMke28) have the same feature.

items.title: Albania
text: The numbers on speed signs are written in a **bold font**.
NOTE: The font is much thinner on speed signs in [Montenegro](https://goo.gl/maps/fvWn6neYoBsnP6J18).

items.title: Austria
text: Austria uses two colour schemes for **chevrons**:
- white on red
- red on yellow
NOTE: Germany mostly uses red on white chevrons, and rarely red on yellow.

items.title: Austria
text: Direction signs have a white background, a **blue outline**, and a unique font.

items.title: Austria
text: Similar white signs with a** **blue outline and unique font can also be seen at the **entrance of towns**.
NOTE: Germany uses [yellow town entrance signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/fLnrUWoSDqzsyGxx5) with a black outline.

items.title: Austria
text: **Green** signs can commonly be seen, giving directions to different local facilities.

items.title: Austria
text: **Pedestrian signs** have a unique design: instead of zebra stripes, they have two horizontal dashed lines.
NOTE: All neighbouring countries have pedestrian signs with zebra stripes.

items.title: Austria
text: Road signs in Austria are sometimes mounted by **four metal clips**, which is unique within central Europe. However, plenty of Austrian signs are attached in other ways.

items.title: Austria
text: **Road markers** are blue with white numbers. They have one decimal separated by a comma, making them very recognizable.
NOTE: Slovenian road markers are white. And German markers have a thin white outline.

items.title: Austria
text: Austrian **bus stop signs** contain a yellow and green circle with the letter **H**.
NOTE: This design is relatively unique in Europe. The only other country with similar bus stop signs is Germany.

items.title: Austria
text: These one-way traffic signs, with the word **‘EINBAHN’** written on them, are unique to Austria.
NOTE: In Germany there will be “Einbahnstraße” written on the sign.

items.title: Austria
text: “No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Austria will often have the words “Anfang” or “Ende” (meaning “beginning” and “end”) written on, or below, them.

items.title: Austria
text: These simple dead-end signs with a **white upside down T** are mostly unique to Austria.
Most countries in Europe use [this sign](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cB2CMCs6fQTNTZPQ8).
NOTE: Older coverage in Switzerland can be seen using [this design](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yv3PkLHesS63WCYD7) as well.

items.title: Austria
text: These **yellow and white stripes** around poles and signposts are found in Vorarlberg.

items.title: Austria
text: **Green** “[Güterweg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCterweg)” signs are found in Burgenland.

items.title: Austria
text: **White** “Güterweg” signs with a **black outline** are mainly found in Upper Austria.

items.title: Austria
text: In Lower Austria, you may find signs with **yellow and blue sign borders**, corresponding to the [flag of the region](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Flag_of_Lower_Austria_%28state%29.svg/2560px-Flag_of_Lower_Austria_%28state%29.svg.png).

items.title: Austria
text: **Vienna street signs** are extremely recognizable dark blue plaques with a traditional-looking white serif font. The number at the start will indicate which district you are in (see the map).
_You can click the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Austria
text: Most other major cities in Austria also have their own **unique street signs**.
NOTE: Many of the arbitrary blue ones can look similar, but the 4 listed in the graphic can be differentiated by:
- Vienna - District Number
- Salzburg - Unique Font
- Klagenfurt - Irregular White Border
- St Polten - Rounded White Border
_You can click the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Croatia
text: Croatia features chevrons with a **red **arrow** **on a **yellow **or **white **background.

items.title: Croatia
text: Croatia has direction signs with a **yellow background** and a **black **outline. They often have a pencil-shaped tip.
NOTE: The other former Yugoslav countries of Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro and North Macedonia have similar signs. A comparison can be seen [here](/images/croatia/croatia_directionsigncomp.png).

items.title: Croatia
text: Croatia’s pedestrian sign features a **pedestrian with a belt** and a zebra path with 5 stripes.
NOTE: The pedestrian on Slovenia’s sign does not have a belt.

items.title: Croatia
text: Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and **Italian** are typically found in Istria, especially in the western cities.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: Bulgaria mainly uses the **Cyrillic alphabet**. However, a lot of signs will also have the Latin alphabet.
The letter “Ъ” is only found in Bulgarian and Russian, although it is fairly uncommon in Russian.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: The Bulgarian word for street is **улица** (ulitsa), sometimes abbreviated **ул.** (ul.).
NOTE: In older street signs seeing only Cyrillic is more common.
Russia also uses улица/ulitsa.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: Bulgarian chevrons are typically **red on white**.

NOTE: Many other European countries have similar chevrons. Crucially, among neighbouring countries, Romania, Turkey, and North Macedonia use the same chevrons. Greece and Serbia use black and white chevrons however. [See this infographic](/images/bulgaria/eu_chevrons.png?) for an overview.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: Bulgarian directional signs are blue, arrow-shaped, and use both the **Cyrillic and Latin** alphabet. Importantly, even if you are far away and cannot decipher the script, you can still see that the sign has two lines of text instead of one.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: Town entry signs have a simple white design and also use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabet. Like with the directional signs, the two lines of text are obvious, even when seen from far away.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: Bulgarian pedestrian signs have **four stripes**, and the person is wearing a hat.
NOTE: No other eastern or central European pedestrian signs have four stripes.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: White street signs with **two red strips**; one covering the bottom and one covering part of the top, can be found in Sofia.
NOTE: You can also find [other types](https://maps.app.goo.gl/EUVuwa83zMGYrP398) of street signs in Sofia.

items.title: Bulgaria
text: **Brown street signs** with bright yellow text can be found in Stara Zagora.

items.title: Denmark
text: Denmark has very unique-looking direction signs that are very useful to recognize the country. They are low to the ground and **framed by pipes**. They are either coloured [red and white](https://goo.gl/maps/xt2jxMHjMQivxS8B7) or [blue and white](https://goo.gl/maps/zC5mi95DGrvhHD8W6), with a directional arrow incorporated into the background. Signs often feature road numbers.

Some larger road signs have a more [standard layout](https://goo.gl/maps/oXjRzsLL2PQBcJC89) without the pipe frame. Highway signs have [blue or green](https://goo.gl/maps/SZ3AQjYCNbzxErT68) backgrounds.

items.title: Denmark
text: Most Danish street names end in **“vej.”** This is the Danish word for “street.” Street signs most commonly have a blue background with white text.

items.title: Denmark
text: This signpost, where the pipe frame is **bent around the sign**, is unique to Denmark.

items.title: Denmark
text: This Danish pedestrian sign has **5 stripes. **Uniquely, the first and fifth stripe touch the edge of the white triangle.
NOTE: Sweden’s pedestrian sign has 4 stripes. Norway almost always has 4 stripes too, but very rarely you can find signs with 5 stripes.

items.title: Denmark
text: This unique sign is found when entering a town. When leaving, there will be a red slash through the sign.

items.title: Denmark
text: Bus stop signs in Denmark are **black and yellow**. A small sign is attached to the top of the pole, with the bus schedule underneath. Additionally, you may see this older [**blue and white**](https://goo.gl/maps/fRjTDJetFmcvkqtt6)** **version.

items.title: Denmark
text: This **red-and-white** chevron is found in Denmark. They are often low to the ground.

items.title: Denmark
text: In addition, these regions each have their own **bus stop sign**.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Denmark
text: These **green bicycle signs** are found on the island of Bornholm.

items.title: Estonia
text: Estonia uses **red chevrons with white arrows.**
NOTE: Russia and Ukraine use the same chevrons.
!!However, Latvian and Lithuanian chevrons have the opposite colour scheme: they are white with red arrows.

items.title: Estonia
text: Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Estonian signs have a **thin** red border, with **no white outline** around it (the red border extends all the way to the edge of the sign).

items.title: Estonia
