text: Estonian pedestrian signs have **3 stripes**. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively high level of detail, detailing **shoes** and an **attached head**.
NOTE: Lithuanian signs also have 3 stripes, but the pedestrian looks less detailed.
!!Latvian pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

items.title: Estonia
text: Estonian bus stop signs have this design.
The bus has **four windows**. This is mostly useful to distinguish it from the Latvian bus stop sign, which has five windows.
Note, however, that Lithuania has the same bus stop signs as Estonia.

items.title: Estonia
text: These **blue and white** signpost wrappings are very common in Estonia.
NOTE: They are also common in Finland and Sweden.

items.title: Estonia
text: Directional signs in Estonia are blue with white text and a white outline.

NOTE: In [Finland](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SsE9X8eTamwvhp1T6), the arrow is built into the white border instead of being an icon inside the border. The arrow on [Latvian](https://goo.gl/maps/g3aqkLH6yjQwrCSF7) signs is more stylized than in Estonia and [Lithuania](https://goo.gl/maps/17A5xxGivFmbs4ae8), where the back part of the arrowhead is vertical.

items.title: Estonia
text: Estonia has a large Russian minority. In most of Ida-Viru County, they form a majority. As a result, you will sometimes see bilingual signs with **Russian Cyrillic** and Estonian in the region in and around Narva.
Note that the majority of signs will still be in Estonian. You may occasionally see Cyrillic in other places.

items.title: Czechia
text: It is common in both Czechia and Slovakia to see temporary square sign posts coated in red and white stripes.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech and Slovak chevrons are **white** with **red arrows**. Less commonly, you may find [red on yellow](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.360934,18.2835385,3a,15y,180.13h,79.56t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1s7hnluRCZ9Kmq_mHW6XJ5AQ!2e0!5s20221101T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) chevrons.

items.title: Czechia
text: Hiking markers, made up of one colourful strip between two white ones, are commonly found in Czechia and Slovakia. They sometimes form an [arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/6XHw2gHa8VDWvhgh7).

NOTE: While by far being the most common in Czechia and Slovakia, similar signs can be found in other European countries such as [Poland](https://goo.gl/maps/aXtx3dQZAxJDEo9u6), [Hungary](https://goo.gl/maps/Rc9N8toac29Zq5Df8) and [Germany](https://goo.gl/maps/W2ek9Z81Qx9ZXStS7).

items.title: Czechia
text: These **black **signs can often be found by the end of bridges in Generation 4 coverage. The road number is displayed on the left.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czechia uses **arrow-shaped** directional signs with a filled in tip. Due to the shape, they are recognizable from [behind](https://goo.gl/maps/Zqsh9W6Fbfyz2VAm8).
NOTE: [Slovakia](https://www.google.se/maps/@48.4606372,17.9419945,3a,15y,86.64h,88.47t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sESbNzDre3j8pPlgC-FhT8A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) has small white arrows instead.

items.title: Czechia
text: The borders of Czech road signs are almost always **separated from the edge** by a strip in the same colour as the sign background.

NOTE: In [Slovakia](https://www.google.se/maps/@48.1580681,17.1258261,3a,24.6y,115.44h,98.53t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sNnRd9IA8rxp5Vc2nYvUN9A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192!5m1!1e4), it is more common for signs to have the border on the edge of the sign.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech highway signs can be either blue or [green](https://goo.gl/maps/fBxJ3iU9UXQPgkjR8), and have a thin white border, which is separated from the edge by a **second** coloured border.

NOTE: [Slovak](https://www.google.com/maps/@48.3562921,18.0491906,3a,21.7y,86.73h,109.67t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sbD26GncxCrFlCaY-jYpwQg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) highway signs have a white border right on the edge.

items.title: Czechia
text: The most common type of street sign in Czechia are **bright red** signs, which can either be wide and stuck on walls, or thin and attached to [signs posts](https://goo.gl/maps/ikgYSMAs1jAg8rqMA). Note that other street signs do occur in some areas, most notably in [Brno](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.1989638,16.6165572,3a,35y,97.05h,95.53t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s4kmt2ZzZOxhdBnJR1Ge13A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192). Similarly designed [blue](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.2119242,15.8240056,3a,15y,292.91h,96.94t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1suOJ7x-GhmeTeCT9Pa6vWng!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) signs are also fairly common.

Furthermore, the Czech word for street is “ulice”, unlike most Slavic languages which use “ulica”. This word is usually omitted, but finding “ulice” on [street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/U6pq8zx1eJPVVHuq9) is still possible.
NOTE: [Slovakia](https://goo.gl/maps/CkdiggTX35tAuRZG8) typically uses white street signs with a red border and blue text.

items.title: Czechia
text: House numbers in Czechia are generally written on **blue** or **red signs** with thin white borders.
NOTE: On the contrary, Slovak house numbers are typically written on [**white signs**](https://goo.gl/maps/arqzJku5JuJJ3CcQ8)** **with a thin red or black border.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech sign posts typically have **thick, black caps**.
NOTE: While some European countries have similar caps, Slovakia usually does not have them.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech pedestrian signs have **five** stripes.

NOTE: The stripes on [Slovak pedestrian signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@48.1706981,17.1749503,3a,15y,50.47h,103.76t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sdNUjkc5XVOND2uDxppzW1A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) are a smaller scale. This is noticeable when comparing the outermost stripes to the edge of the triangle.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech road signs have a fairly** thin font**.

NOTE: [Slovak](https://www.google.se/maps/@48.6121158,17.8343458,3a,15y,35.68h,88.71t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s7V5Bac7DZqw_gIaMTTy6zw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) signs normally have a much bolder font. The same font is however used in [Luxembourg](https://goo.gl/maps/G2VWXYozceB7FjgD6) and [Germany](https://goo.gl/maps/S4zvN55HUprvgY6n8).

items.title: Czechia
text: Bicycle signs in Czechia are yellow. You may also find markings similar to hiking markers, but with [yellow stripes](https://goo.gl/maps/toztoSy8i79p6pNk8) instead of white.

items.title: Czechia
text: Czech railway crossing signs do **not** have a background.

NOTE: [Slovak](https://www.google.se/maps/@48.5221855,17.4540175,3a,15y,74.7h,97.77t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sD6lspMXwIUgsJJU74xCt6Q!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) railway crossing signs have a white rectangular background.

items.title: Czechia
text: While possible to find in most of the country, **blue street signs** are more common in the east of the country, with Ostrava being the only major city to mainly use them.

items.title: Czechia
text: If you see a white street sign with **blue text** and a **red border**, the same as is typical for Slovakia, then you should be near the Slovak border.

items.title: Czechia
text: White street signs with **red text** are most commonly found in the eastern parts of the country. They can also be found in the southernmost parts.
NOTE: Brno notably uses this design.

items.title: Czechia
text: White street signs with **blue text** are most common in the eastern parts of the country, but can also be seen in the central northern parts.

items.title: Czechia
text: White street signs with **black text** are most commonly found in the southeastern parts of the country. Note that these can look very similar to the ones with blue text.

items.title: Czechia
text: Polish bilingual street signs are found in Český Těšín, and very rarely in other [nearby towns](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.5752315,18.7627604,3a,15y,178.22h,95.37t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s99563llRkK9adal39xiU6w!2e0!7i16384!8i8192).

items.title: Czechia
text: The street signs in Šumperk can be recognized by being blue, with **text** filling out almost the **entire sign**.

items.title: Faroe Islands
text: Directional signs are **yellow** with a **thin black border** and a metal frame, very similar to the ones in [Iceland](https://maps.app.goo.gl/5HsMnQt8A7fSwKpo6).

items.title: Gibraltar
text: The main language used in Gibraltar is **English**. This can be especially helpful if you see English on official signs in a Mediterranean setting.
NOTE: Note that English is also one of the main languages of Malta, which also has a Mediterranean landscape and vibe.

items.title: Finland
text: Most Finnish street names end in “**tie**” or “**katu**.” These are the Finnish words for road and street. Street signs most commonly have a white background with black text.
NOTE: You may find roads ending in “polku” and “kuja”.

items.title: Finland
text: Finnish road signs have a **yellow background**.
NOTE: Signs in Sweden and Iceland also have yellow backgrounds. Norway, however, has signs with a white background.

items.title: Finland
text: On traffic signs that have a red border, you will find a thin **yellow stroke** on the edge of the sign.
NOTE: You will not see this in any other Nordic country.

items.title: Finland
text: Finnish pedestrian signs have **5 stripes**.
NOTE: Pedestrian signs in Sweden and Norway **usually** have 4 stripes. In [rare cases](https://goo.gl/maps/wMS7W2CWGyAi4DJt9), you can find 5 stripes in Norway.

items.title: Finland
text: Finnish **directional signs** consist of a solid blue background, white text, and a white border with guiding arrows.

items.title: Finland
text: Finnish chevrons are **black with yellow arrows**.
NOTE: Norway and Iceland have similarly coloured chevrons. Sweden, on the other hand, has unique blue and yellow chevrons.

items.title: Finland
text: Traffic signposts often have **blue and white** striped markings.

NOTE: This pattern can also be found in Sweden. While the same colour scheme is also common in [Estonia](https://www.google.com/maps/@58.3430383,26.7407475,3a,22.2y,264.88h,67.51t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sP587UApP9JnjyawxVML4YA!2e0!7i13312!8i6656), the markings typically have a wider shape and attach to the signpost in a looser way.

items.title: Finland
text: Finland has two styles of **bus stop signs**, a blue and white one, and a yellow and black one.

NOTE: This can be used to tell Finland apart from Sweden, which has many different bus stop signs ([example](https://goo.gl/maps/h4BWBzQgVu4mtNgr6)), most of which have the names of the stops on them.

items.title: Finland
text: Finnish regional roads have 3- or 4-digit road numbers. The **first digit** of those road numbers is **region-specific**. These regions are distributed in a rough south-to-north order, starting from 1 in the south to 9 in the north.
These road numbers often appear on direction signs. Learning the regions can help with cutting down on scanning time for 5k’s, or give you a rough region to plonk in during quick no move games.
NOTE: Major roads with 2-digit road numbers do not adhere to this geographic pattern.

items.title: Finland
text: The [**Sámi languages**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1mi_languages) are spoken in the far north of Finland. In this region, you can sometimes find bilingual signs with place names in both Finnish and Sámi. Unlike Finnish, its alphabet uses the letter **c**.

items.title: Finland
text: Some pedestrian signs on Åland have **four stripes**, with the exact same design found in Sweden. Beware that many pedestrian signs will still be the typical Finnish design.

items.title: Finland
text: Bus stops on Åland include a **white plate** with 4 numbers. Some also include this semicircle sign on top.
NOTE: Some bus stops in Mariehamn do not follow this rule.

items.title: Finland
text: You can find **Red rectangular metallic plates** with 7 golden or dark red coloured protrusions that form a rounded hexagon shape on houses, lamp posts, and signposts in Tampere.

items.title: Finland
text: This style of **blue street sign **with white text is unique to the cities of Seinäjoki and [Isokyrö](https://goo.gl/maps/SdmNDAwLzkXPyN6z6) southeast of Vaasa.

items.title: Finland
text: Lahti uses these street signs with a **black border** and all capital letters.

NOTE: You can rarely find similar signs in other cities, but Lahti almost exclusively uses this design. Notably, Kuopio can use these [signs](https://goo.gl/maps/wjdzkPYj7ba2NRGN7), which use a thicker, more compact font.

items.title: Finland
text: The city of Kerava uses street signs with this **blue-**and-**yellow **[coat of arms](https://fi.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keravan_vaakuna#/media/Tiedosto:Kerava.vaakuna.svg) in the top-left corner.

items.title: Finland
text: The city of Järvenpää uses street signs with this **blue-**and-**grey **[coat of arms](https://fi.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A4rvenp%C3%A4%C3%A4n_vaakuna#/media/Tiedosto:Jarvenpaa.vaakuna.svg) in the top-left corner. The [neighbourhood](https://media.discordapp.net/attachments/1045971390202925086/1063500707099070514/Jarvenpaan_Alueet.png) name is also written above the street name.
NOTE: If you see a street sign with a coat of arms not mentioned in this guide, you should be near Kerava or Lahti.

items.title: Hungary
text: Hungarian chevrons are **white on red**.

[Black-and-white](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.2517674,16.9392096,3a,37.6y,261.49h,65.38t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1s_Vx5ThXqoem-sKrW96OMFw!2e0!5s20111101T000000!7i13312!8i6656) chevrons may also be seen, but are considerably less common.

items.title: Hungary
text: Hungarian sign posts commonly appear to be **abnormally tall**, often taller than the Street View camera.

items.title: Hungary
text: Hungarian signs are usually bolted to the sign post using **four bolts**, going through the sign, in the shape of a tall rectangle.
NOTE: This is not common in any other Eastern European countries.

items.title: Hungary
text: Hungarian pedestrian crossing signs have **five stripes**. The person is wearing a **belt**. There is also a second, less common, type with four stripes and the person holding a bag.
The belt is located noticeably **low** on the person’s body, almost as if the person is sagging his pants. This is unique to Hungary.
NOTE: Among neighbouring countries, Croatia and Slovakia also have five stripes and a belt.

items.title: Hungary
text: Apart from European highways, there are two types of numbered roads in Hungary; roads marked with **green signs**, and highways beginning with the letter ‘**M**’, marked with **blue signs**. These road numbers are contained within a small shield shape on the sign.

items.title: Hungary
text: Most directional signs are green, having a white inner border and a green outer border. Directional signs on M-numbered highways are blue, having a white inner border and a blue outer border.

items.title: Hungary
text: If you see a street sign with a **thick metal frame** around it, you are very likely to be in the **western** parts of the country.

items.title: Hungary
text: If you see a **blue** or **green** street sign shaped like an **arrow**, attached to a utility pole or street light, you are likely to be in the county of Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg.

NOTE: Blue arrow-shaped street signs can also be found in [Dunakeszi](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.6290186,19.1549932,3a,29.7y,151.87h,90.55t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1se_1iRMK0jnxi0R13E9x-8A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192), north of Budapest. However, those are attached to blue sign posts.

items.title: Hungary
text: This infographic showcases ten of the largest towns and cities with **unique street signs**, and explains what makes them unique.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

items.title: Greece
text: Greek chevrons have **white arrows** on a **black background**.
NOTE: Similar chevrons are found in Albania, Italy and the UK. Spain has the same colours, but will almost always have either two or four arrows.

items.title: Greece
text: Greek warning signs have a red border and a **yellow background**.

items.title: Greece
text: Greek directional signs are typically blue and arrow shaped. One of the most recognisable features are the place names, which are written in Greek with a **yellow font**, and in English with a white font.

items.title: Greece
text: Greek town entry signs are white with thick **horizontal blue stripes** at the top and bottom.

items.title: Greece
text: Pedestrian signs have **two dotted horizontal lines**, rather than vertical stripes.

items.title: Iceland
text: The road direction signs of Iceland are **yellow**. They usually have a white inset box that shows the road numbers. If the inset box has a dashed border, the number listed refers to a nearby road, not the road you are currently on.
NOTE: Direction signs for very local destinations, such as farmsteads, typically have different background colours: blue or white.

items.title: Iceland
text: Icelandic pedestrian signs feature **four stripes** and often have a **slight yellow tint**.
NOTE: Iceland is the only European country that uses pedestrian signs with a yellow background.

items.title: Iceland
text: Iceland’s street signs use a white background and black text. They often have a **thin metal rim** and are attached to lampposts or traffic lights.

items.title: Iceland
text: Icelandic chevrons are **black with yellow arrows**.
NOTE: Norway and Finland have similarly coloured chevrons. Sweden, on the other hand, has unique blue and yellow chevrons.

items.title: Iceland
text: Just like Sweden and Finland, Icelandic signs feature a **yellow background**.

items.title: Iceland
text: Iceland has a very sensible **road numbering system** that allows for quick 5k’s, provided you find the yellow direction signs that list the road numbers of the intersection you are on.
The main ring road, which circles the entire island, simply has the number 1. There are no other roads that start with 1.

The first digit of the other road numbers is region-specific. These regions have a sequential distribution around the island, starting from 2 in the south and increasing up until 9 in a clockwise direction (see map for approximate distribution).

items.title: Iceland
text: Barren landscapes consisting mostly of** dark volcanic gravel**, with little to no vegetation or signs of life, are typical of the inland regions of Iceland. Most such covered roads are located in the east.

items.title: Germany
text: Germany also has a wide variety of sign backs. Notably, you can commonly find **black** or **dark grey** sign backs, which are rather rare in Europe. Most signs will also feature this sticker, with an upside-down red triangle on a black rectangle.
NOTE: Italy, Romania and Albania also have black sign backs, however landscape should be sufficient to tell them apart.

items.title: Germany
text: German town entry signs are **yellow** with black text and have a **metallic frame**.
NOTE: These signs can include a lot of useful information too:
- !!The town and/or city name on the top.
- !!The Municipality in the middle.
- !!And the county on the bottom.

items.title: Germany
text: German pedestrian signs have **five stripes** and the person has a **belt**.
NOTE: The same design is used in Luxembourg.

items.title: Germany
text: These one-way traffic signs, with the word ‘**Einbahnstraße**’ written on them, are unique to Germany.
NOTE: In Austria, there will be “EINBAHN” written on the sign.

items.title: Germany
text: “No Stopping” and “No Waiting” signs in Germany will often have **white arrows** drawn on them.

items.title: Germany
text: **Bicycle direction signs** typically feature a white background with green lettering. In Hamburg, North Rhine-Westphalia and a neighbouring part of Lower Saxony, you will instead find red lettering. The Saarland has its own distinctive design, with white text on a dark green background.

items.title: Germany
text: You can use the backs of street signs to regionguess Germany.
Here are examples of a [folded](https://goo.gl/maps/edxgzquC6mXrySvh9), and [flat](https://goo.gl/maps/5cw4KiWCdgYQXFzy7) sign back.

items.title: Germany
text: You can also use the sign back connectors on street signs to regionguess Germany.
NOTE: The double connector on triangular signs are generally [wider](https://goo.gl/maps/zNwkDqQkt5vCVAGx7). T-shaped connectors may look like [this](https://goo.gl/maps/ru72EcB1fE3dt8zZA).

items.title: Germany
text: - [Berlin](https://goo.gl/maps/byoGqSgok1uhmjCy6) uses white signs with a grey border, and a separate section for numbers under the street name. Also note how the letter ß looks.
- [Munich](https://goo.gl/maps/RMshmDUSNucokmWN9) has blue street signs with a white decorative border that does not touch the corners. Also note the unique font.
- [Stuttgart](https://goo.gl/maps/fPFeuNukTiRTWoki7) uses **black** signs without a border.
- [Düsseldorf](https://goo.gl/maps/L9kbaYYwzV2iFE9n9) has **black** signs with a white border, similar to Munich. The signs have a **metallic frame.**
- [Dortmund](https://goo.gl/maps/3PhsxrNkq7oduns59) uses blue signs with a white border and a grey frame. The signs also have a separate section for numbers under the street name.
- [Essen](https://goo.gl/maps/wXngUHVBa2eS9CH2A) has blue signs with a very **thick** metallic frame.
- [Dresden](https://goo.gl/maps/S83P48x1grRfYR8H8) has blue signs with a unique font.
- [Hanover](https://goo.gl/maps/4oWah3dfDGep5sR6A) uses white signs with a **wider** than usual gap between the sign and metallic frame.
- [Nuremberg](https://goo.gl/maps/fUp3W4uEMsbFGtYH6) has blue signs with a unique font. The signs also have a grey frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- [Wuppertal](https://goo.gl/maps/SUe7ExCD7S7SJDye7) uses white signs with a unique font and a white painted frame with a small gap between it and the sign.
- [Mainz](https://goo.gl/maps/bj8Mt4jAxn9duXodA) has a mix of blue signs, and this unique **red** variant.
- [Frankfurt ](https://goo.gl/maps/FDzr8ZLrSehrSAoC8)uses blue street signs with a metallic border around the sign, as well as the separate section for numbers under the street name.
NOTE: More rarely, some smaller towns can use similar signs to those in this graphic.

items.title: Germany
text: [Sorbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbian_languages), a **Slavic** language, is spoken near the Polish and Czech border. You can find it on a variety of signs in these regions.

items.title: Germany
text: Every city state uses a unique and recognisable bus stop.
- Berlin uses **segmented** bus stops, with a **yellow** signpost.
- Hamburg bus stops have a **red signpost**, and the route numbers are within **hexagons**. Note that they can be found outside of Hamburg as well.
- Bremen proper uses simple bus stops, which have the bus stop name within a **red section**. The edges can be rounded.
- Bremerhaven, which is still part of Bremen, uses bus stops with a **grey section** on the opposite side of the signpost. And the bus stop name is **red** within a **yellow** section.

items.title: France
text: Small **yellow signs** displaying the road number, which typically starts with a “**D**”, are unique to France. They are commonly placed on top of directional signs or town entry signs.

items.title: France
text: French directional signs are usually white with a black outline slightly offset from the edge. They have an arrow-like shape, with the black border getting thicker at the point.
Highway directions have either a [blue or green background](https://goo.gl/maps/8jKUAjSqdf9AJcLM9).
Smaller places and points of interest are frequently written in an italic font.

items.title: France
text: Town entrance signs in France have a red border with a thin white outline.

items.title: France
text: French road signs have a red border with a thin white outline. You will often find white rectangular signs with black text below traffic signs.
NOTE: Road signs in Spain have a [thick red border](https://maps.app.goo.gl/49ec9Xf89vko3Tbr5) that goes all the way to the edge.

items.title: France
text: Many traffic signs in France have flat rectangular signposts.
_Signposts, along with signbacks, can be dyed with unorthodox colours, more so than in other countries. Some of those are regional, which you can learn more about in the regionguessing section._
NOTE: The only other European countries with flat signposts are Portugal, Spain, and Andorra.

items.title: France
text: Traffic signs with particularly **short signposts** are very common in France.

items.title: France
text: France uses chevrons with white arrows on a blue background. They can have a wide amount of arrows, ranging from one to five.
NOTE: The only other European country with this colour scheme is Spain, where you will only find chevrons with two or four arrows.

items.title: France
text: Pedestrian crossing signs in France have five stripes and a disconnected head on the person. They have the usual white border of French traffic signs.
Less commonly, you can find a design with [two dashed lines](https://goo.gl/maps/iD7GdGUA7Ew3h8oa7) instead of stripes.

items.title: France
text: Kilometre markers in France most commonly have a yellow or red semicircle on top of a white rectangle. They can be found in the form of a waystone or as a flat sign and can be either [parallel](https://goo.gl/maps/8KpoMhXGetkA7qeR9) or [perpendicular](https://goo.gl/maps/WJHfU8tnG9qfZoyDA) to the road. Major highways can have [square markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RTdHYF79SdUZFLTt7) with a red top.

items.title: France
text: Roads may be lined by tall rectangles on a stick in the colours of the Austrian flag, which are not found elsewhere.

items.title: France
text: House numbers in France are most commonly blue, typically written in a serif font with slightly exaggerated shapes. This is most useful when differentiating from Italy, which almost never uses blue house number signs.
NOTE: Similar designs can be found in all other neighbouring, as well as many other, countries.

items.title: France
text: Most departments have their own unique logo (formally called official flag), often containing stylized initials or the entire name. Notable infrastructure with department logos include [bus stops](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1CqFWtzhUqLV2k8n7), [kilometre markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JGY1Xwa8SvPyyV5A9), [trail banners](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kP4kjMrH3rK5gLSZ7), [directional signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QM5gqNqrRtf4gWRR6) and [signbacks](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZHA8UMQL6eFzSNyP6). Learning what each logo looks like is not recommended for beginners, but it can be helpful to know what they stand for when scanning.

You can find the full list of logos [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_the_regions_of_France#French_Departments), or see them projected onto a map [here](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/06/Flag_Map_of_Departments_of_France_Version_2_%28Logo_Flags%29.png).

items.title: France
text: A flag made up of red and yellow stripes, based on [the Senyera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senyera), is the official flag and department logo of **Pyrénées-Orientales**. You will often find the pattern used in coats of arms on street signs.
NOTE: The flag of [Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provence) looks similar, but with [vertical](https://maps.app.goo.gl/CWTzNJaQNoRJwEDeA) stripes instead.

items.title: France
text: **Dark green** road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.
NOTE: Beware that this, and the following coloured infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

items.title: France
text: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a **green sticker**, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

items.title: France
text: Still in Eure-et-Loir, this is also where D-roads with a **superscript number** are most common. On the map, these are expressed as decimals, e.g. D134.10 and D121.9.
NOTE: They are rarely found in other [departments](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FLC24eo6tV36Jn1D8).

items.title: France
text: A **greyish green** signback supported by a **darker green** post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

items.title: France
text: In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a **dark green post** paired with a signback of a **lighter shade of green**, ranging from [matcha green](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cH9cbEYkyVwUMkEXA) to [greenish turquoise](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HVwoK8mut3XwKQ8g8). The [department’s logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/fr/6/64/Logo_62_pas_de_calais.jpg), a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present [on the signback](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RV2AH3h7Lq75MKu47).
NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs mentioned in the previous tip.

items.title: France
text: Road signs where both the** post** and **back** are painted **brown** are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is **square**, however round signposts are equally common.

items.title: France
text: Directional signs in Haute-Garonne often use **burgundy red attachments** and ornaments. This is sometimes paired with [yellow signposts](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zXUbPBqqsHJZaBvu7).

items.title: France
text: Most town entry signs in Marne follow a unique format: Instead of having [separate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/MK8LGR6zFBcdyG2M7) entry and exit signs, they are combined into a **single, noticeably thicker block**.

items.title: France
text: Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the** name of the city**, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a **modern design**, and many city names will be** river based**, notably named after Seine and Marne.
NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

items.title: France
text: [**Breton**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language) is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include **d**, **k**, **w **and the letter** ñ**, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as [Rennes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SXA9tpudgXLcbpvJ7) and rarely [Nantes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/v9hAN6FqvpLekm5n6). The Breton word for street is straed**.**

items.title: France
text: [**Alsatian**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsatian_dialect), a dialect of German, is occasionally found in [Alsace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace), a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.
NOTE: Streets [containing German names](https://maps.app.goo.gl/jEGWQJfdTYS2sMK18) are also concentrated in this region, though not as consistently.

items.title: France
text: [**Occitan**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occitan_language) is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on [town entry signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/J5Bj9ZSR2MfHAegg9). It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal** **dialect.
Click [here](https://i.imgur.com/B8gX96p.png) for a more extensive infographic.
NOTE: The street sign designs pictured are also unique to the two cities respectively.

items.title: France
text: Bilingual signs in [**Basque**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_language), a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a **thinner font**, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

items.title: France
text: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in [**Corsican**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsican_language), a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings** u/iu/ju**, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.

items.title: France
text: **Paris**, **Lyon** and **Marseille** are the three largest cities in France and the only ones divided into **municipal arrondissements **(Arrᵗ or Arrt.** **for short). The arrondissements appear on google maps, so finding these street signs can help a lot with pinpointing.
The street signs of these three cities will be further described in the following tips.

items.title: France
text: Paris uses an iconic** green & Prussian blue **design with a top arch that has also been replicated in [Bucharest](https://maps.app.goo.gl/E3LqAPwX8jt9YmgK8), which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.
NOTE: The simple rectangular form of the sign can be found in the [towns nearby](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Noo6GyM9T63fta8C8) and rarely in [other cities](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SN1rqVG9eMNqQZxQ8).

items.title: France
text: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an **uninterrupted inner white border** that cuts a **notch** for the arrondissement and each bolt.
NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the [name of the suburb](https://maps.app.goo.gl/gP3ngUUpUKf4Rqmz6) instead.

items.title: France
text: **Marseille**’s street signs will usually feature the city’s **emblem**, a variation of the [Greek cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_cross_variants#Greek_cross). The white border will usually be **interrupted** at the top, even when the cross is [absent](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Kb4vaENAKeNfGt2XA).

items.title: France
text: Small tables with “**Arrᵗ**” written on a small separate sign, are found in **Bordeaux**, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

items.title: France
text: **Montpellier** street signs will typically contain a blue **‘M’** on a white background in the top left corner.

items.title: France
text: Street signs with a red slanted [fleur-de-lis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleur-de-lis) are unique to **Lille**.

items.title: France
text: In the outskirts of **Bordeaux**, you may find square traffic signposts with the [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_red#Claret) shade of **red**, named after the wine grown in the region.
NOTE: Red posts by themselves are not unique to Bordeaux, so apply this meta with caution.

items.title: France
text: On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as **Blue Coast**), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, [Cagnes-sur-mer](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sP2LGFRxb79XRWro6), west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.
NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly [Brittany](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6GwpcWAD5gS5LCE7A), so consider the landscape as well.

items.title: Cyprus
text: A former crown colony of the United Kingdom until 1960, Cyprus continues to use some **borrowed infrastructure**, like signs and roadlines. This is also why Cyprus drives on the **left**, and why** English** is so widely used.

items.title: Cyprus
text: Directional signs are very similar to Greek directional signs, with the one notable difference being that the Greek text is written in **all-caps**.

items.title: Cyprus
text: Town entry signs consist of either a yellow rectangle with a red border, or just the smaller white rectangle that contains the town name in both Greek and English. The signs will also contain a speed limit sign above them. These designs are unique to Cyprus.

items.title: Cyprus
text: Cyprus uses four-digit postal codes, grouped by region. They can be [found on street signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QLKgfjhF61xNEmVu9), and are denoted by either T.K. or T.T.
The first digits can be useful to memorise.

items.title: Cyprus
text: With a Russian-speaking population of around 17%, many commercial signs in Limassol feature **Russian **translations.

items.title: Isle of Man
text: Many street signs in Ramsey feature the** oval shaped coat of arms**.

items.title: Isle of Man
text: The** coat of arms** is placed** above the text** on many signs in Port Erin.

items.title: Ireland
text: Ireland is the only European country that uses yellow **diamond-shaped** warning signs.
Note that this only applies to warning signs. Regulatory signs (circles and upside down triangles) have the normal red border and white background, like most other European countries.

items.title: Ireland
text: Irish chevrons are **yellow on black**. Both single and multiple arrows are common.
NOTE: UK chevrons are white on black.

items.title: Ireland
text: Irish yield signs feature the word “**YIELD**”.
NOTE: UK yield signs have the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

items.title: Ireland
text: Pedestrian crossing signs are somewhat rare in Ireland. They are yellow and diamond-shaped, like other road signs.
Instead of pedestrian signs, you will often see these **black and white signposts** with a yellow bulb on top.
Note that the UK uses exactly the same signposts.

items.title: Jersey
text: In general, road infrastructure is **similar **to that found in the United Kingdom. This includes driving on the [left](https://goo.gl/maps/fcPxAUuyzEzRf9Ak7), as well as [directional signs](https://goo.gl/maps/kNsowiMi9Dd68QKt5), [chevrons](https://goo.gl/maps/NBkNUYfGXL1baFQr8) and [warning signs](https://goo.gl/maps/dK5pbVjsHtbSjTAo6). Some of the subtle differences are discussed below.

items.title: Jersey
text: Due to its proximity to France, the vast majority of street and locality names contain **French **words. The island’s traditional language, known as [Jèrriais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A8rriais), is closely related to French and appears on some [signs](https://goo.gl/maps/gfXPVEU3CehwnLD79).

items.title: Jersey
text: Jersey has an extensive network of cycling routes. Most notably, you will find [signs](https://goo.gl/maps/i9MW5htcqMZYhqRq9) referencing the start or end of a **“Green Lane”**. Blue [**route markers**](https://goo.gl/maps/kqz88wFjRsujGHFx5), containing a map of the island in the centre, are also common.

items.title: Jersey
text: Some road signs are **asymmetrically **attached to their signposts. This appears to be more prevalent on Jersey than on the British mainland.
NOTE: Keep in mind that this only applies to a minority of signs. Most are attached regularly.

items.title: Jersey
text: Most street name signs in Jersey are adorned with the **coat of arms** of the parish in which they are located.
_You can click on the graphic to enlarge it._

items.title: Latvia
text: Latvia uses white chevrons with red arrows.
NOTE: Many other European countries, including Lithuania and Poland, use the same chevrons.
!!However, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine use chevrons with the opposite colour scheme: red with white arrows.

items.title: Latvia
text: Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Latvian signs have a **thick** red border, with a **thin white outline** around it.

items.title: Latvia
text: Latvian pedestrian signs have **five stripes**, which is unique within the Baltics. Uniquely, the pedestrian has noticeably **long legs** compared to pedestrian signs in other European countries.
The other two Baltic countries have three stripes on their pedestrian signs.

items.title: Latvia
text: Latvian bus stop signs have this design.
Most importantly, the bus has **five windows**. Within the Baltics, this is unique to Latvia. The other two Baltic countries have four windows.

items.title: Latvia
text: Latvian directional signs are blue with white text.

NOTE: The arrow on Latvian signs is more stylized than in [Estonia](https://goo.gl/maps/eW7AJWdVriTfsprx7) and [Lithuania](https://goo.gl/maps/17A5xxGivFmbs4ae8), where the back part of the arrowhead is vertical.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Bus stops in Liechtenstein use a **green-and-white** design, with a black metallic border around the sign. The phrase LIEMOBIL is written at the top.
NOTE: The metallic frame is not always black.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Like Switzerland, directional signs in Liechtenstein are generally white (smaller roads) or blue (bigger roads), and they have a pointed arrowhead, with a contrasting colour.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Liechtenstein pedestrian signs have **seven stripes**. The signs also have an oddly tall rectangle.
NOTE: Switzerland uses identical signs.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Road signs in Liechtenstein commonly have a round, grey **metal border** around them.
NOTE: Swiss and German signs can also have similar metallic borders.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Unlike the rest of Liechtenstein, Vaduz sometimes uses **red bus stop signs.**
NOTE: ** **Regular bus stops are also present.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Unlike the rest of Liechtenstein, Balzers sometimes uses **black bus stop signs.**
NOTE: ** **Regular bus stops are also present.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Blue street signs with a thin white border will place you either in the south of Liechtenstein or in the north around Bandern.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Blue street signs that don’t have an outline are found in Eschen.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Flat black signs are found in eastern Liechtenstein.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Black signs with a white border and embossed letters can be found in Schaan.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: These brown street signs with a font reminiscent of **traditional German typefaces**, along with a white border, are found in Vaduz and the northern towns.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Brown street signs that have an **arrow design** are unique to Ruggell.
NOTE: The regular brown signs are also present in Ruggell.

items.title: Liechtenstein
text: Browns signs which have a more ‘generic’ font will place you in Planken.

items.title: Lithuania
text: Lithuania uses **white chevrons with red arrows**. The small single chevrons (pictured here) usually have a **red outline** on the edge of the sign.
NOTE: Many other European countries, including Latvia and Poland, use the same chevrons (though without the red outline).
!!However, Estonia, Russia and Ukraine use chevrons with the opposite colour scheme: red with white arrows.

items.title: Lithuania
text: All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker. However, they can be distinguished from each other by their angle relative to the road.
In Lithuania, the marker will be at a **45° angle** towards the road. The sign itself has an L-shape.
For a quick overview of all three Baltic countries, see [this infographic](/images/lithuania/baltics_kmmarkerinfographic.png).

items.title: Lithuania
text: Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Lithuanian signs have a relatively **thin** red border, with a **thin white outline** around it.

items.title: Lithuania
text: Lithuanian pedestrian signs have **3 stripes**. The shape of the pedestrian has a relatively low level of detail.

NOTE: Both [Russia](https://www.google.com/maps/@55.7423905,37.5885686,3a,15y,227.43h,93.29t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sM2IafnQY_X5LJKXlumRVzQ!2e0!6shttps:%2F%2Fstreetviewpixels-pa.googleapis.com%2Fv1%2Fthumbnail%3Fpanoid%3DM2IafnQY_X5LJKXlumRVzQ%26cb_client%3Dmaps_sv.tactile.gps%26w%3D203%26h%3D100%26yaw%3D122.40399%26pitch%3D0%26thumbfov%3D100!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) and [Ukraine](https://goo.gl/maps/KBnV7gubZHs349dc8) share the same design.** **[Estonian](https://goo.gl/maps/5vqjNxsfM1wHnxSw5) signs also have 3 stripes, but the pedestrian looks more detailed.
!!Latvian pedestrian signs have 5 stripes.

items.title: Lithuania
text: Lithuanian bus stop signs have this design.
The bus has **four windows**. This is mostly useful to distinguish it from the Latvian bus stop sign, which has five windows.
Note however, that Estonia has the same bus stop signs as Lithuania.

items.title: Lithuania
text: The Lithuanian word for street is **gatve**, often abbreviated as **g.** on signs and Google Maps.
This word is almost entirely unique to Lithuanian. However, very rarely, you might see ‘gatve’ (abbreviated as gat.) in the Latvian capital of Riga.

items.title: Lithuania
text: Lithuanian directional signs are blue with white text.

NOTE: The arrow on [Latvian](https://goo.gl/maps/g3aqkLH6yjQwrCSF7) signs is more stylized than in [Estonia](https://goo.gl/maps/eW7AJWdVriTfsprx7) and Lithuania, where the back part of the arrowhead is vertical.

items.title: Lithuania
text: In Generation 3 coverage, you will often see **random small blurs**. These blurs look similar to the ones that are used to blur out licence plates or faces, but instead they cover seemingly random parts of the image – often on direction signs.
NOTE: This is also common in the Russian oblast of Kaliningrad, just to the southwest of Lithuania.
!!These random blurs are not typically found in Estonia or Latvia.

items.title: Lithuania
text: Rarely, you can see bilingual signs with **Polish language** in a small area southeast of Lithuania.
Note that this is by no means very common, but it can help with getting very close guesses if you do see bilingual Polish-Lithuanian signs in an otherwise obvious Lithuanian setting.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: Chevrons are **black with yellow** arrows. You may also rarely come across [blue and yellow](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.6287886,6.1349694,3a,15y,1.97h,71.47t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s64mNrisMtRf0qKgQ49PAaw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) chevrons.
NOTE: None of Luxembourg’s neighbours use these chevrons.
The only other European countries with this colour scheme tend to have wildly different landscapes: Iceland, Norway, Finland, Ireland, and Portugal.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: Luxembourg is a highly **multilingual country**. It has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, French, and German.
French is the language that is mostly used for public communication. Road signs and advertisements are usually in French.
Presence of German on signs is less common compared to French, but certainly not non-existent.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: **Directional signs **are yellow with a thin black outline. Town names are written in uppercase. The signs have a pointed tip. They are completely surrounded by a **frame**, making them very recognizable.
Some directional signs feature road numbers:
- Regional road numbers have 1 or 2 digits and a red box.
- Local road numbers have 3 digits and a [yellow box](https://goo.gl/maps/vunmzYKY3iy5bEGk6).

items.title: Luxembourg
text: **Town entrance signs **are also yellow and surrounded by a frame.
Most of these signs have bilingual versions of the town name. They frequently have the road number on the top, along with a speed limit sign.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: Almost all Luxembourgish road signs will be supported by a **white signpost**.
NOTE: While not nearly as common, white signposts are also found in [France](https://maps.app.goo.gl/rYufTJHHu99ALVKf6).

items.title: Luxembourg
text: **Street signs** are almost always short and usually have a white background. The exact designs vary from town to town.
A very common design is the one pictured on the left in the example image, with slanted blue corners.
NOTE: Belgian street signs often appear short as well, but can have other background colours – not just white.
In addition, Dutch street signs almost always have a blue background and tend to be much longer than they are tall.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: Some signposts have this bulky, round reflector with **blue and white** markings.
NOTE: Similar markings are found in Sweden and Finland. Landscape should be sufficient to tell these apart from Luxembourg, however.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: **Pedestrian signs** have 5 vertical stripes.
NOTE: Belgian pedestrian signs have 2 horizontal stripes.

items.title: Luxembourg
text: **Bus stop signs** are blue and always have this exact design. The bus has six windows.
NOTE: Bus stop signs in Belgium and the Netherlands have significantly different designs. For example, the Belgian bus stop sign always has a [yellow signpost](https://goo.gl/maps/HRqx4mPFRvtkV2u2A).

items.title: Italy
text: Italian is the most spoken language in Italy. It uses many double consonants, and typically has a very large number of i’s. You can also find ì, é and à. Most words will end with a vowel.
NOTE: The Italian word for street is ‘via’, and can be found on most street signs.

items.title: Italy
text: It is very common for the back of Italian road signs to be **black**, or dark grey.

items.title: Italy
text: Directional signs are **blue** with a **white arrow**. All letters on these signs will be **capitalised**.

items.title: Italy
text: Directional signs in national roads (Strada Statale) are **blue** with a **white and blue border**.
Divided highways (Autostrade) have **green** signs with a **white and green border**.

items.title: Italy
text: Italian kilometre markers are white squares with a **roman numeral** on top and an arabic numeral on the bottom. The arabic numeral gives you the number of kilometres and the roman numeral gives you the number of hundred metres from the start of the road.

items.title: Italy
text: Italian road numbers will normally begin with the letters “SS”, “SR” or “SP”.
The second letter can be used to identify the type of road.
- "S" when it is a State road, so the number is unique within the country.
- "R" when it is a Regional road, so the number is unique to the region.
- "P" when it is a Provincial road, so the number is unique to the province.

items.title: Italy
text: Italian chevrons are **white arrows** on a **black background**.
NOTE: In Southern Europe, white on black chevrons can also be found in Spain, Greece and Albania.

items.title: Italy
text: Street signs are typically white with a thin **blue border** and **black text**.

items.title: Italy
text: Italian pedestrian signs have **five stripes** and a basic person without a belt.

items.title: Italy
text: These signs, featuring a “no parking”-sign with the text “**passo carrabile**” are commonly found in urban areas. At the top of these signs you will typically find the municipality (comune) name.

items.title: Italy
text: The region of South Tyrol has a German majority, and as such uses **German bilingual signs**.

items.title: Italy
text: **French** can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.

items.title: Italy
text: Close to the Slovenian border you can find **Slovene bilingual signs**.

items.title: Malta
text: The Maltese word for street is “**triq**”, which can be seen on almost every street sign.

items.title: Malta
text: These **blue signs** are unique to Valletta.

items.title: Montenegro
text: Montenegro uses **black on white** or **red on yellow** chevrons.
NOTE: Albania uses white on black chevrons.

items.title: Madeira
text: Since Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles and chevrons.

items.title: Madeira
text: Bus stops signs on Madeira follow a unique **black, white **and** yellow** colour scheme.

items.title: Madeira
text: These speed limit signs are unique to Madeira and can be found on its highways.

items.title: Madeira
text: Signposts on Madeira are often striped.
NOTE: These are also seen on the Azores.

items.title: Madeira
text: You can sometimes find **free roaming cows** on high-altitude roads on the island, as well as warning signs for those cows. The cows will typically be brown with white spots, contrary to the Azores, where the cows will typically be [black and white](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vsM6TJ2DnHi1vKEG7).

items.title: North Macedonia
text: Direction signs in North Macedonia are typically **yellow **with** biscriptal text**: town names are written in both Latin and Cyrillic script.
NOTE: Serbia, Slovenia, Croatia, and Montenegro have similar signs. Serbia is the only one that will have biscriptal text though.

items.title: North Macedonia
text: Macedonian is a Slavic language which uses the **Cyrillic** script. Road signs have Latin on them too, although most other signs are fully in Cyrillic.
The letters ‘**Ѓ**’ and ‘**Ќ**’ are unique to Macedonian. ‘Љ’, ‘Њ’, and ‘Џ’ are only in Serbian and Macedonian.

items.title: North Macedonia
text: North Macedonia normally uses **yellow-filled** **in warning signs**. Most of Europe uses white ones.
NOTE: In southeastern Europe, Greece also commonly uses yellow-filled in signs. Slovenia sometimes has yellow-filled signs.

items.title: Poland
text: Warning signs are triangular and have a **yellow background** and a distinct **thin red border**.
NOTE: In Europe, this combination of a yellow background with a thin red border is unique to Poland.

items.title: Poland
text: However, prohibitory signs are round and have a **white background** with a thicker red border.

items.title: Poland
text: Poland has a unique **pedestrian sign**. Instead of the usual zebra stripes, it just has a single horizontal line.
NOTE: Austria and Belgium also have horizontal lines, but they use two lines instead of Poland’s single line.

items.title: Poland
text: Regular Polish direction signs have a **green background**. These signs use a distinct font, which is a good clue for Poland.
NOTE: Signs on expressways have a blue background.

items.title: Poland
text: Poland has two **town entry signs**: a green one with the locality’s name, and a white-and-black one with a stylized urban area.
NOTE: Like direction signs, town entry signs use a distinct font.

items.title: Poland
text: Polish chevrons are **white with red arrows**.

items.title: Poland
text: **Regional** **roads** have 3-digit road numbers. These numbers often appear in yellow boxes on direction signs. The first digit is usually region-specific, as there is a high level of geographic clustering of these road numbers.
There is some overlap between numbers near the margins of the regions. Some exceptions also exist.
NOTE: This tip only applies to 3-digit roads. Bigger roads with 2-digit road numbers mostly do not adhere to this geographic pattern.

items.title: Poland
text: While rare, bilingual signs can be found in the highlighted regions.
- **Kashubian**, found in the north, is another West Slavic Language, featuring a lot of umlauts and accents.
_Wszëtczi lëdze rodzą sã wòlny ë równy w swòji czëstnoce ë swòjich prawach. Mają òni dostóne rozëm ë sëmienié ë nôlégô jima pòstãpòwac wobec drëdzich w dëchù bracënotë._
- **German** is mostly found in the Opole Voivodeship.
- **Lithuanian **can be found around Puńsk, near the Lithuanian border.
- **Belarusian** is found near the Belarusian border.
- **Lemko, **another Cyrillic language, can be found in the southeast.

items.title: Poland
text: Białystok uses **turquoise** street signs, with the district marked on the bottom.

items.title: Poland
text: Szczecin uses colourful **green** and **blue** signs. The city district is marked on the bottom.

items.title: Poland
text: Street signs in Poznań are mainly **black**, with the district being marked on the blue section at the bottom.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Street signs are almost always **blue with white lettering**. Very rarely, you can find [yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/yMhbRKLJK1QuyEs68), [white](https://goo.gl/maps/8TuTmC7n7oLw8qAS9) or [green](https://goo.gl/maps/W3BrcUwTrYA4TeMC8) street signs.

The Dutch word for street is **straat**. Other common road name endings are -weg, -laan, -pad, and -plein. However, if you see a blue sign with the word ‘fietspad’, do not search for it; it simply means ‘bicycle path’.
NOTE: Street signs in Belgium come in a variety of colours and usually mention the municipality, which is rare in the Netherlands.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Dutch **direction signs** are blue with white lettering. Signs for bicyclists are [white with a red border](https://goo.gl/maps/Ym8jxRtVRgdeJFgf6).

items.title: Netherlands
text: Dutch **town entry signs** are blue. The signs sometimes have very [elaborate designs](https://goo.gl/maps/XAfoVPzYZfX83KoS9), often with frames and additional signs.

NOTE: Often, these signs list the municipality they are in, after the word ‘gemeente’ (gem). Many municipalities are named after larger towns or cities in the vicinity, which can help a lot with scanning.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Edges of Dutch road signs will extend to the back, creating a **border visible from behind**, sometimes retaining the colour of the sign. This is both consistent and unique to the country.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Many Dutch signposts feature **striped markings** with a black-and-white or blue-and-white colour scheme.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Road signs on traffic islands often have these bulky **yellow signposts**.

items.title: Netherlands
text: Some road markers (“**hectometre markers**”) have province-specific designs. This only applies to markers for regional N-roads, which have road numbers in yellow boxes.
Not all N-road markers have province-specific designs: some just have a generic design that can be found nationwide.
The A-roads all have the same signs and are recognizable because the road number is in a red box.
Bollards sometimes feature **kilometre stickers**, which are also limited to specific regions.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it. Image provided by Timzkii._

items.title: Netherlands
text: In the province of Friesland, the Frisian language is commonly spoken. While Dutch language is still most prevalent on signs, a lot of town entry signs will feature **bilingual town names**.
Some street names in Friesland uniquely end in -wei or -strjitte.

NOTE: Frisian has vowels with [circumflex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumflex) diacritics (“little hats”): Â, Ê, Ô and Û. Dutch does not have these letters, except in loanwords. In addition, the Y is significantly more common compared to Dutch.

items.title: Netherlands
text: **Amsterdam street signs** feature the city district in a smaller font size below the actual street name.
NOTE: This design is very uncommon in the rest of the Netherlands.

items.title: Netherlands
text: The municipality of Oegstgeest, just northwest of Leiden, uses uniquely illegible street signs with** yellow text on a red background.**

items.title: Netherlands
text: **Baarle** is a town in the south of the Netherlands which contains a number of Belgian enclaves. Throughout the town, you can sometimes see signs of this, such as markings on the pavement and [Dutch and Belgian flags](https://goo.gl/maps/sKCBPk8vqM9AUrmB9) being flown together.

items.title: Portugal
text: **Hunting signs** with a red and white colour scheme are a common sight in rural areas. They are either diamond shaped or rectangular.

NOTE: In contrast, [Spanish](https://www.google.com/maps/@39.9083771,-2.5360346,3a,15y,154.88h,76.9t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1se3LYRFex8eXCgocKMCvxPw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) hunting signs are white and black.

items.title: Portugal
text: Directional signs are generally white, with **black arrows** that are **not** touching the borders of the sign.
NOTE: [Spanish](https://goo.gl/maps/NdKZE9FwK2q66enj6) directional signs will typically feature the road number in colourful boxes and do not have a black arrow, other than a thin black border.

items.title: Portugal
text: Most kilometre markers are wide rectangles with a **coloured section** on the left side divided diagonally from the white part. Every kilometre you will find a larger [square sign](https://goo.gl/maps/d31pnwB3RjC8JZWD8) with a coloured top half featuring the road number.

items.title: Portugal
text: Stop signs in Portugal feature a fairly large font.

NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish it from [Spain](https://www.google.com/maps/@41.4989864,-1.390895,3a,15y,67.65h,81.9t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sPtHx268nIZR2fqVugwTlsQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu), where stop signs have a distinctly small and compact font.

items.title: Portugal
text: Portuguese chevrons are **black with yellow arrows**.
NOTE: Portugal is the only Mediterranean country with this chevron colour scheme.

items.title: Portugal
text: Pedestrian signs have **five stripes**, and the person is wearing a **belt**, which is noticeably high.

NOTE: [Spanish pedestrian signs](https://goo.gl/maps/tsQ3wkTxKwZuebwp9) have eight stripes, [Italian signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RiDqBuojwMhYqgDCA) don't have a belt and [Greek signs](https://goo.gl/maps/RCxiJ5SWmjfFM3TB8) have two dotted lines instead of stripes.

items.title: Portugal
text: Portuguese road signs are typically encased by a **white border**.
NOTE: Most [Spanish](https://www.google.com/maps/@38.8639722,-4.7943486,3a,17.5y,29.06h,88.7t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1swJ7te-wPHR9taiHRqU2LIg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) signs don’t have a white border.

items.title: Portugal
text: **Lime green street signs** can be found in Porto.

items.title: Norway
text: Norwegian pedestrian signs typically have **four stripes** and a very simply drawn person. Note however, that there is a version with [five stripes](https://www.google.com/maps/@69.6519241,18.9565431,3a,15y,247.79h,95.06t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sr44nQpcvP6QQiIoQ5x9iPg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) and a version where the person is more detailed and [wearing a hat](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.9150958,10.7314409,3a,15y,221.76h,97.28t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sxUjNRfgz1D4jn2MrTFqN3A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192).

NOTE: While [Finnish](https://www.google.com/maps/@61.4993731,23.759534,3a,15y,50.36h,98.09t,359.73r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sklmrQCHLp2po9CQARyRyMA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) pedestrian signs have five stripes, Swedish pedestrian signs have four stripes. However, the person on [Swedish](https://www.google.se/maps/@59.8459127,17.6306563,3a,15y,112.66h,95.96t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s-ODCYQW5xsTcVebPn08xRQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) signs is detailed, but without a hat.

items.title: Norway
text: Norwegian directional signs are **yellow** with a **black border**. You will commonly see the road number displayed, either in a green box for European highways and major roads, or in a white box, for smaller roads.

items.title: Norway
text: On smaller roads, it is common to see these blue signs with a **large white M**.

NOTE: Similar signs can be found in [Sweden](https://goo.gl/maps/DqYAkha51nY72ao49), however the font is distinctly different. The middle point of the M does not extend to the bottom of the letter. There are no similar signs in Finland.

items.title: Norway
text: Norwegian bus stops usually have this small, **blue sign** with a white bus.
NOTE: Sweden has a lot of different bus stops, none of which look like this.

items.title: Norway
text: **White signs** with the text “**Sone**”, generally featuring a speed limit, are common in urban areas.

items.title: Norway
text: Street signs will generally be **centred** on top of sign posts.
NOTE: Street signs in Sweden will normally be attached either to the side of [sign posts](https://goo.gl/maps/YnsWJyWT27GYkDXGA) or [lamp posts](https://goo.gl/maps/JyeS5LBN8nZDyKrt8).

items.title: Norway
text: Norwegian traffic signs have a red outline and a **white background**.

NOTE: Both [Swedish](https://www.google.se/maps/@60.2182208,17.4734016,3a,15y,311.3h,89.49t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1spg1fT6h2pXchIZ0XtF9UHA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) and [Finnish](https://www.google.com/maps/@65.00534,25.5795144,3a,15y,139.16h,87.81t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s17sGKjC9XHOAQHw_NCoL_A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) road signs have a yellow background.

items.title: Norway
text: You can also find these road construction signs, with a **bright yellow** background.

items.title: Norway
text: Most smaller road signs will be attached with four visible **sign bolts** in the shape of a tall rectangle. Beware that you may occasionally find [framed signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@58.8495149,5.7367006,3a,21.3y,31.15h,97.95t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sXRj68ZaFOCOFubBo1k50Nw!2e0!5s20221001T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) instead, particularly in urban settings.

items.title: Norway
text: Norway uses **yellow on black** chevrons.

items.title: Norway
text: Small **white square signs**, displaying the road number on top, and the distance to the closest town, are common to see along medium sized roads.

The road number will be preceded either by an R or an [F](https://www.google.se/maps/@62.2252395,6.269883,3a,15y,195.25h,79.98t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sz50wFAvEtsVFmAutPi8UBQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192). F roads show up as Fv on the map and are generally difficult to locate, while R roads lack any letters on the map and are generally more findable.

items.title: Norway
text: Bilingual signs with **Sámi** can be found in several northern areas in Norway. While the Sámi languages are very different from Norwegian, the best way to recognize them are the letters Á, Đ and the use of several vowels in a row, something which is uncommon in Norwegian.
Note that not all signs in these areas will be bilingual.

items.title: Norway
text: **Russian** can sometimes be seen alongside Norwegian on signs near the Russian border. It is mostly found on roads E6 and E105 near Kirkenes.

items.title: India
text: India typically has **black and white striped signposts**.
NOTE: Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka also have black and white signposts.

items.title: India
text: The City of Chandigarh is a **planned industrial city**. As a result, the city features a lot of unique infrastructure, such as [blue signs](https://goo.gl/maps/HAYdSmx9sEsf2kbZ8) mentioning sectors and industrial areas, round yellow markings on street lights, and [street signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@30.7499192,76.7780503,3a,16.1y,130.5h,95.4t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sPVs101xGkIhtQvDG4dwKtA!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) which will typically feature [several numbers](https://www.google.com/maps/@30.7250865,76.7767257,3a,15y,43.08h,74.38t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1shEU9Ii83j_XOg74Ltm5G1Q!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) rather than street names.

NOTE: The nearby cities of [Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar](https://www.google.com/maps/@30.7021706,76.7282816,3a,15y,307.52h,103.68t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sq0D20ET6KxQ-CQ2ZRgdqog!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) and [Panchkula](https://www.google.com/maps/@30.6802307,76.8513495,3a,15y,85.06h,89.37t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sOcviMvOxgJKg32g23wdDhg!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) are also planned industrial cities, which feature somewhat similar signs.

items.title: Mexico
text: Mexican directional signs have a distinctly large, **all-caps** white font.

items.title: Mexico
text: Mexico uses the word “ALTO” on stop signs.
NOTE: All of South America, as well as Puerto Rico, use the word “PARE”. Panama, Costa Rica, and Guatemala also use “ALTO”.

items.title: Mexico
text: Arrows on signs are noticeably **very thick**.

items.title: Mexico
text: Similarly, Mexican **postal codes** can be seen on this map. They will commonly appear at the [bottom of street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/8bgZx7q8pjzzFSYi6), and are ordered alphabetically based on state names.

items.title: Mexico
text: A thick **cross** can be seen on the back of signs in Chihuahua.

items.title: San Marino
text: Road signs and bollards are **generally identical** to the ones used in Italy.
NOTE: Many road signs give directions to the nearby Italian city of **Rimini**.

items.title: San Marino
text: San Marino is the only country in the world to use **yellow **chevrons with **burgundy red **arrows.

items.title: San Marino
text: These **elaborate pedestrian crossings**, with painted blue crosswalks and hanging signs, are specific to San Marino.

items.title: Serbia
text: Serbia uses chevrons with a **black arrow** on a **white** background.
NOTE: Within Europe, these chevrons can also be found in Slovenia, Montenegro and North Macedonia.

items.title: Serbia
text: **Bilingual signs** with Serbian alongside Hungarian can be seen in northern Vojvodina, where there is a Hungarian majority.

items.title: Romania
text: Romanian directional signs are blue, arrow shaped, and have a white border. They will very often display the **road number**, which can be either **red or **[**blue**](https://goo.gl/maps/62EzegUJUrbSQHwQ6).

items.title: Romania
text: The most common type of town entry sign in Romania is a **yellow sign** displaying a speed limit and a city skyline, with a **white sign** displaying the town name below.

NOTE: The upper sign can also either be [white](https://goo.gl/maps/nAGuvAEn4CDn1iQu5) or [completely absent](https://www.google.com/maps/@43.9295577,23.865666,3a,15y,60.5h,84.85t,358.78r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sXfkr8gj25si9PKl8IgR9Ew!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu).

items.title: Romania
text: Romanian sign backs are often **black**.
NOTE: This is also common in Italy, Albania and Germany.

items.title: Romania
text: Romanian chevrons are **red on white**, often with a **yellow frame**.
NOTE: Several eastern and central European countries have the red on white chevrons, however yellow frames are by far the most common in Romania.

items.title: Romania
text: This yield sign, with an extremely **thick red border**, with a **thin white outline**, is unique to Romania. Beware that different yield signs also exist in Romania.

items.title: Romania
text: Bilingual signs with **Hungarian** are mostly found in the central regions of Covasna, Harghita and Mureş, but also less commonly near the Hungarian border.

items.title: Romania
text: Several Romanian cities and towns have **unique street signs**. This infographic covers all with a population above 100 000.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Slovenian directional signs are **yellow** with a **black border**.

NOTE: Croatia, North Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro all have similar directional signs. [Austrian](https://www.google.com/maps/@46.5568458,13.9585166,3a,17.9y,222.77h,88.58t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sgiePX811VzIqDTkzzrcHsw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) directional signs are typically white with a blue outline.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Slovenian chevrons usually have **red arrows** on a **white background**.
You can also find a less common [version](https://maps.app.goo.gl/3rjSbRq9SMVina6a7) with a **black arrow** on a **white background**.
NOTE: [Austrian](https://goo.gl/maps/BM8aPY3HC9ox4UNHA) chevrons are either white on red or red on yellow.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Slovenian pedestrian signs have **five stripes** and a simply drawn person without a belt.
NOTE: [Austrian](https://goo.gl/maps/S3nXofrbfKot9eLD6) pedestrian signs have two dotted lines, while the person on [Croatian](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yy9Gf53S8AH7Areg6) signs has a belt.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Slovenian street signs are most commonly white with a **metal border** attached to signposts, or **red** and attached to house walls.

NOTE: [Czech](https://goo.gl/maps/gi5f8C9LNAUumAQFA) street signs are also typically red and attached to walls. However, Czech street names will not contain the word “ulica”, which most Slovenian street names have.

items.title: Slovenia
text: **Italian bilingual signs** can be found in the westernmost region.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Instead of the normal red house numbers, Ljubljana will typically feature **green house numbers**.
NOTE: [Street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/h5GSwk121qRJantj8) in Ljubljana are also occasionally green.

items.title: Slovenia
text: Street signs in Celje feature the emblem of the city, a blue shield with **three yellow stars**.

items.title: Svalbard
text: **Russian** can sometimes be found on signs.

items.title: Slovakia
text: It is common in both Slovakia and Czechia to see temporary square sign posts coated in red and white stripes.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovak and Czech chevrons are **white** with **red arrows**. Less commonly, you may find [red on yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/mGXmo2VFj1MSUCXw7) chevrons.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Hiking markers, made up of one colourful strip between two white ones, are commonly found in Slovakia and Czechia. They sometimes form an [arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/rdpAP15NABRWY6J59).

NOTE: While by far being the most common in Slovakia and Czechia, similar signs can be found in other European countries such as [Poland](https://goo.gl/maps/aXtx3dQZAxJDEo9u6), [Hungary](https://goo.gl/maps/Rc9N8toac29Zq5Df8) and [Germany](https://goo.gl/maps/W2ek9Z81Qx9ZXStS7).

items.title: Slovakia
text: These **black **signs can often be found by the end of bridges in Generation 4 coverage. The road number is displayed on the left.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovakia uses [blue directional signs](https://goo.gl/maps/2mkRyA6uUbEVFavi7), with **small** **white arrows**.
NOTE: [Czechia](https://www.google.se/maps/@50.1064121,14.913933,3a,15y,60.44h,88.2t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1so99PGzeEpfVrMqGK8iZJAg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) has large filled in white arrows instead.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovak road signs commonly have the painted sign border right **at the edge** of the sign.
NOTE: The borders on [Czech signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/DjWmV787QcRDvfqd6) are almost always separated from the edge of the sign by a strip in the signs background colour.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovak highway signs can be either blue or [green](https://maps.app.goo.gl/d3DyfWrkuaqj8KdeA), and have a white border right **at the edge** of the sign.
NOTE: The borders of [Czech](https://maps.app.goo.gl/xCNCvayFVSTaWKYh9) highway signs are separated from the edge.

items.title: Slovakia
text: White street signs with **blue text** and a **thin red border** are by far the most common in Slovakia.
NOTE: The same design can also be found in Czechia, near the Slovak border. However, Czech street names **never** feature the word “ulica”.

items.title: Slovakia
text: House numbers in Slovakia are typically written on **white signs **with a thin red or black border.

items.title: Slovakia
text: The top of Slovak sign posts are typically either open, have a [grey metal](https://goo.gl/maps/VHA8WCG3dJw9XWtW7) cap or a [thin black](https://goo.gl/maps/JYFx95Mmcoq6HvZBA) cap.
NOTE: Most [Czech](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.0862812,14.4369725,3a,49.6y,111.31h,103.69t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1siU7X9kVnn5rpAk12DE47pA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) sign posts have a thick black cap.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovakia uses two major pedestrian signs, both having five stripes. The first has a simply drawn person with a belt, and the second has the stripes very close together.

NOTE: The same belted design is found in [Germany](https://goo.gl/maps/JswrpY6bbBQYzAmy8). A similar design, with a distinctly lower belt, is found in [Hungary](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dk233SspcTiQGdeG6). While very rare, pedestrian signs with similarly condensed stripes can also be found in Czechia.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovak road signs normally feature a very [**bold font**](https://www.google.se/maps/@48.4928647,17.9733382,3a,15y,218.15h,88.03t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sY8wARZiZIiQjgt3CYNxqSg!2e0!5s20220801T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu).
NOTE: The font on [Czech](https://www.google.com/maps/@50.1047918,14.8557813,3a,15y,16.35h,81.93t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sCynHQszUMJnLGBkvq608pQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) signs is much thinner.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Slovak cycling signs use the letter **C** as their symbol, unique to the country. They’re visually analogous to the Czechoslovak hiking markers mentioned in step 1.1, including the [yellow post](https://maps.app.goo.gl/CG99xS8ZvRjQEERg8) on directional signs.

items.title: Slovakia
text: The Slovak railway crossing sign has a white **rectangular background**.
NOTE: [Czech](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.9821592,15.293333,3a,15y,252.56h,95.32t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1seauodxqef41k7Ijnp-XHVA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) railway crossing signs do not have a background.

items.title: Slovakia
text: It is fairly common to see small signs with **double sign posts** in Slovakia.
NOTE: While large signs may have double sign posts, small signs rarely do in Czechia.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Several areas in southern Slovakia have a **Hungarian majority**, with bilingual street and information signs.

items.title: Slovakia
text: In the northeastern parts of the Prešov region, you may find bilingual town entry signs in [Rusyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusyn_language), a Cyrillic based language closely related to Ukrainian.

items.title: Slovakia
text: Skalica, in the northwestern corner of the country, has **red street signs**, similar to the ones commonly found in Czechia. However, the somewhat stylized font distinguishes it from the Czech signs.

items.title: Switzerland
text: The colour of **directional signs** indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white.

Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a [white sign](https://goo.gl/maps/pfJ2QNrPFmB7q6xN9).

items.title: Switzerland
text: Swiss pedestrian signs have **seven stripes**, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.
NOTE: Liechtenstein uses identical signs.

items.title: Switzerland
text: Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey **metal border** around them.

NOTE: [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wbSfjB8xPexuUkqZA) uses almost identical directional signs. Somewhat similar metal borders are found on some directional signs in [Denmark](https://goo.gl/maps/gQWu5BCRsga8WkiS7).

items.title: Switzerland
text: Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually **white or blue**, with a **metal frame** around them.

NOTE: On the back of these signs you may often find the distance to larger, nearby cities. Furthermore, the abbreviation for the canton can often be seen on the bottom of the sign, especially when the town is situated near a canton border.

items.title: Switzerland
text: **Chevrons** are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are [white with a black arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/S8YmmUW2vnbEQryN9).
NOTE: Austrian chevrons are red and white, or red and yellow.

items.title: Switzerland
text: These bus stop signs, with thick **metal signposts** going around them, are unique to Switzerland.

items.title: Switzerland
text: The text on the **speed limit signs** varies depending on the official languages in the region.

items.title: Switzerland
text: **Cantons** are the first-level administrative division of Switzerland. It is very common to find the two-letter abbreviation for the canton that you are in, as seen on some town entry signs. As such, remembering these can be a great asset when region-guessing Switzerland.
NOTE: If you happen to come across an [unblurred licence plate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yi7rVDEFGXqwZaWSA), the first two letters will correspond to the canton that it is registered in.

items.title: Switzerland
text: These **large** town entry signs can sometimes be found in the canton of Vaud.

items.title: Switzerland
text: **Olive green infrastructure**, particularly signposts, sign borders and sign backs, are found in Basel-Landschaft.

items.title: Switzerland
text: These blue street signs, with **rounded edges** on the sides, are unique to the city of Sankt Gallen.

items.title: Switzerland
text: Large blue street signs, attached to a **low double signpost**, similar to directional signs in [Denmark](https://maps.app.goo.gl/234Fd9GSuZQRtH47A), are found in Basel.
